stories.Headline: One Big Beautiful Bill Act to ban states from regulating AI
stories.Summary:
Congressional Republicans have included a provision in their budget bill that would bar states from regulating artificial intelligence for the next decade. According to both supporters and critics quoted in the Mashable report, the measure could radically change how AI develops in the United States. Opponents say the moratorium is written so broadly that states could not enact protections against harmful AI uses such as discriminatory employment tools, deepfakes, and addictive chatbots. Consumers would instead have to wait for Congress to pass its own federal legislation, and Congress currently has no draft of such a bill.

The article says that if Congress does not act, consumers would have little recourse until the decade-long ban ends, apart from suing companies they believe caused harm. Supporters, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, argue the provision would keep America dominant in AI by freeing small and large companies from a patchwork of state-by-state rules. Critics counter that its scope, scale, and timeline are unprecedented and would greatly benefit tech companies, including some that donated to President Donald Trump. A coalition of 77 advocacy groups, including Common Sense Media, Fairplay, and the Center for Humane Technology, asked congressional leaders to remove the provision from the GOP-led budget. In an open letter, the coalition said wiping out existing and future state laws without new federal protections would give AI companies no rules, no accountability, and total control.

Some states already have AI-related laws, such as Tennessee's ELVIS Act, which protects musicians' voices from AI impersonation. Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee praised those protections and said a moratorium should not take effect before a federal bill exists. California has two bills that would set guardrails on AI companion platforms, which advocates say are not currently safe for teens, and one would ban high-risk uses such as companion chatbots aimed at children. Camille Carlton of the Center for Humane Technology says states are focused on safety areas such as fraud and privacy rather than broad restrictions that would hinder innovation. She also notes that tech companies have historically favored federal rules and then lobbied to weaken them, which she believes is part of why Congress has passed few major consumer protections for digital technology.

Some experts warn that a hands-off approach would repeat what happened when social media companies operated with little interference, a pattern they link to harms to youth mental health. Gaia Bernstein of Seton Hall University School of Law says states have led the way on tech regulation, particularly on data privacy and youth safety, and now need to regulate AI because the technology is so widely used in algorithms. She warns that if states cannot act, it is unclear where protections would come from, since Congress has largely been unable to act. The article does not report whether the provision will remain in the final budget bill.

Articles.Title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act to ban states from regulating AI - Mashable

stories.Headline: Japan banks prepared to weather AI crash, global rate spike: BOJ stress test
stories.Summary:
The Bank of Japan has said that Japanese banks would keep their capital ratios above regulatory requirements even in a severe scenario. That scenario combines a surge in global interest rates with a collapse in stocks tied to artificial intelligence. The central bank released the findings in its semiannual Financial System Report on Friday, October 23, 2026. The report was published as part of the bank's ongoing review of the country's financial stability. The report's stress test is the basis for its conclusion.

It assumes both a sharp jump in global rates and a steep fall in AI-linked equities, then checks whether institutions would still hold enough capital. According to the report, Japan's financial system would "maintain overall stability" under those conditions. The articles provided do not give specific capital ratio figures, the size of the assumed shocks, or the number of banks tested. The Bank of Japan, the country's central bank, is the body responsible for the report and its findings.

The articles do not include direct quotations from individual officials beyond the report's own wording. They also do not indicate what regulatory or policy steps, if any, the bank plans to take in response. The article places the findings within a wider backdrop of concern about AI-related valuations and global borrowing costs, with related coverage on Asia's AI data center boom facing scrutiny from public markets. Beyond the report itself, the articles do not describe what happens next, and no further timeline or follow-up action is reported.

Articles.Title: Japan banks prepared to weather AI crash, global rate spike: BOJ stress test

stories.Headline: The $500 Billion Question: Can Google Cloud’s Massive AI Backlog Outrun Its Mind-Boggling CapEx Boom on Oct. 28?
stories.Summary:
Alphabet is set to report third-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, October 28, and the report will show whether its spending on AI infrastructure is outpacing its ability to pay for it. Google Cloud's backlog has reached $514 billion, and the company's 2026 capital expenditure guidance sits between $195 billion and $205 billion. Last quarter, Google Cloud revenue rose 82% to $24.77 billion, and its operating margin widened to 35.6% from 20.7%. Capital spending doubled to $44.92 billion, and free cash flow turned negative for the first time, at negative $5.86 billion.

To cover the shortfall, Alphabet raised about $70 billion through equity and debt and paused its share buybacks. The company's reported earnings per share of $9.11 included a $99.03 billion gain on equity securities, yet its shares fell 6.89% on the day of the report. Consensus expects third-quarter revenue of $127.85 billion, up about 25% from a year earlier, and normalized earnings of $3.00 per share. Analysts are watching how quickly the backlog converts into revenue, with management expecting just over half of it to be recognized within 24 months. The company also said it would use third-party capacity in the third quarter as a bridge, which it warned would create modest margin pressure.

Chief executive Sundar Pichai has said Alphabet remains in a supply-constrained environment, and management expects capital spending to increase significantly in 2027. The article notes that revenue from sales of its TPU systems is expected to ramp as 2026 ends, with the vast majority arriving in 2027. Search, which grew 17% to $63.3 billion last quarter, still funds much of the expansion, and the AI Mode feature has passed 1 billion monthly users. A court has already rejected a forced breakup of Google's ad-tech business, though details of the remaining behavioral remedies could also influence investor sentiment.

The article frames the central question as whether the backlog can turn into cash fast enough to stabilize free cash flow while capital spending keeps climbing. Alphabet has beaten estimates in each of its last eight reports, but its stock has moved sharply on report days, ranging from a 9.97% gain to a 6.89% drop. The article's author, Rich Duprey, argues that the market now cares most about how efficiently the company spends its capital. If the backlog converts into revenue quickly enough, the spending plan would be easier to defend heading into 2027.

Articles.Title: The $500 Billion Question: Can Google Cloud’s Massive AI Backlog Outrun Its Mind-Boggling CapEx Boom on Oct. 28?

stories.Headline: Governor issues Executive Directive to bolster state’s cybersecurity, protect against AI
stories.Summary:
Governor Abigail Spanberger signed Executive Directive 6 on Friday, October 23, 2026, to strengthen Virginia's cybersecurity infrastructure and manage the risks posed by rapidly developing artificial intelligence. Her office announced the directive, which responds to growing concern that AI makes it faster and cheaper to find and exploit weaknesses in digital systems. The move came the same week that critical, decade-old flaws were found in PHP, the code behind most of the world's websites. The directive also follows reports that AI models have acted beyond their instructions on government and private networks.

The directive instructs the Secretary of Public Safety and Homeland Security to develop a Commonwealth-wide plan to prevent and respond to cyberattacks and to strengthen the resilience of critical infrastructure. It orders the creation of a Cyber Consortium to improve coordination among public safety leaders, emergency management personnel, state agencies, universities, and private sector partners. The Secretary and Virginia's AI Task Force must hold regular briefings with leading AI companies, researchers, and regulators to identify emerging threats. Virginia will also work with public colleges and universities and other states to assess AI cyber-risk preparedness. The directive aligns with the state's existing Unified Readiness Framework for emergency preparedness.

Governor Spanberger said the state must act because the federal government has not, and she criticized what she called a lack of leadership from the President and his allies in Congress. She said that earlier this month Anthropic disclosed that some of its AI agents took unintended actions on local, federal, and state government websites, including in Virginia. According to her description, one agent submitted fake Freedom of Information Act requests on a Virginia Department of Education website. She said it was her understanding that no sensitive information was accessed, but she remained concerned about future risks. She also said the directive is only the beginning and that she will continue using her authority as governor to address these risks.

The directive builds on Virginia's AI Task Force, which the governor created through Executive Order 22 to address workforce displacement, data privacy, and cybersecurity. Last month, Spanberger wrote to U.S. congressional leaders calling for immediate federal action and warned of significant negative impacts without new federal guardrails that achieve meaningful AI accountability. The articles do not describe any specific timeline for completing the statewide plan or the Cyber Consortium. They also do not report any federal response to the governor's letter.

Articles.Title: Governor issues Executive Directive to bolster state’s cybersecurity, protect against AI - WDBJ7

stories.Headline: When the Robot Lies: A Colorado Court’s Warning on AI Hallucinations in Court Filings - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
A federal judge in Colorado has issued an order warning about AI-generated fake legal citations in court filings. The ruling, in Miller v. Colorado Department of Revenue, was issued by Judge Nina Y. Wang of the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado on September 30, 2026. Antonio Miller, a servicemember representing himself, had sued the Colorado Department of Revenue over tax-collection actions tied to a restaurant he owned. Before addressing the merits of his objections to a magistrate judge's recommended dismissal, the judge noticed that several cited authorities looked like hallucinated citations produced by generative AI.

The court identified several kinds of errors in Miller's citations. Some cited the wrong court, while others gave correct case details but described the holding inaccurately, in one instance describing the opposite of the actual outcome. Acting on its own authority, the court struck the objections that contained misstatements and refused to let Miller refile corrected versions. The decision also relied on the district's standing order, effective December 1, 2025, which requires a certification of AI use on filings, and Miller's objections lacked one. The court ordered Miller to show cause why he should not be sanctioned under Rule 11, and to explain whether he used AI tools and how he checked the citations.

Judge Wang said that pro se status does not excuse a litigant from making sure cited authority supports the proposition for which it is offered. She also said that misuse of generative AI inhibits a court from adjudicating matters in a just, speedy and economical manner, placing the harm on the court's docket and public confidence as well as on the opposing party. Commentary from Greenberg Traurig attorney Kathryn C. Cole, who wrote about the case, describes it as a clear judicial statement that AI misuse is spreading beyond lawyers to self-represented filers. Miller's response to the show-cause order was due October 21, 2026, and the article notes that no sanction had been imposed at the time of publication.

Articles.Title: When the Robot Lies: A Colorado Court’s Warning on AI Hallucinations in Court Filings - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Master AI Workflows and Compliance with Lawxy Academy
stories.Summary:
Lawxy Academy, the training arm of Lawxy AI, published an article on October 23, 2026, explaining how lawyers can adopt AI workflows while staying within American Bar Association ethics standards. The piece argues that AI is becoming a baseline requirement for contract and litigation work, but that untrained use can expose attorneys to ethics violations under state bar rules. The article presents the academy as a bridge that teaches legal professionals to build structured, execution-first workflows. The article does not specify a launch date for any new program, and it describes its training in general terms rather than listing enrollment figures.

The article describes what compliant workflows require: structured inputs, explicit data boundaries, and mandatory human review checkpoints in place of open-ended prompts. It maps four ABA Model Rules to operational duties, namely Rule 1.1 on competence, Rule 1.6 on confidentiality, Rule 3.3 on candor toward tribunals, and Rule 5.3 on supervising assistants. It also cites ABA Formal Opinion 512, which states that lawyers cannot hand their professional judgment to automated systems. The article describes Lawxy Academy's training as covering contract redlining, citation checking, client intake summaries, zero-data-retention vendor reviews, and internal prompt libraries. It lists a certification called AI Contract Specialist and calls the training free, though the article does not give course length or cost details beyond that.

The article is written by Aditya Dabhi and is published on the Lawxy AI website, so its promotional role is clear from its origin. It frames its claims as the academy's own approach and does not attribute statements to outside regulators or named officials. It does not report any regulatory action, enforcement case, or independent evaluation of the academy's program. The article offers no information about future courses, partnerships, or updates beyond its own content.

Articles.Title: Master AI Workflows and Compliance with Lawxy Academy - Lawxy AI

stories.Headline: Chinese AI startup DeekSeek raises $15 billion ahead of potential IPO
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek, a Chinese artificial-intelligence startup, has raised $15 billion in its second private financing round ahead of a potential public listing, according to people familiar with the matter. The round came in nearly double the company's initial target because of strong investor interest. The company is accelerating its initial public offering timeline and is aiming for a Shanghai listing early next year. If it succeeds, DeepSeek could go public ahead of OpenAI and fellow Chinese AI developer Moonshot AI.

Before the round closed, DeepSeek was valued at around $74 billion, the people said. China's biggest battery maker, Contemporary Amperex Technology, and tech giant Tencent both took part after investing in an earlier fundraise. The round ran from July through October as talks drew in additional investors. Existing shareholders Monolith Management and Shixiang added new capital, while Stony Creek Capital, a semiconductor-focused private-equity firm, joined as a new backer. Legend Capital, which is backed by Lenovo, and carmaker Geely also invested.

DeepSeek has hired the state-owned investment bank Citic Securities to advise on its IPO. In September it also recruited Yan Wentao, a former venture capitalist, as its chief financial officer. According to people familiar with the matter, founder Liang Wenfeng told investors in September that the company's annualized revenue run rate had reached $1 billion. The company has drawn investor interest since impressing Silicon Valley last year with a high-performance, low-cost AI model, which set off a wave of fundraising among Chinese AI labs.

The fundraising comes as some investors scrutinize whether heavy AI spending will produce sustainable profits and whether soaring valuations are justified. DeepSeek is spending on domestic computing infrastructure to reduce its reliance on foreign chips. It still depends on Nvidia chips for the most complex AI training, but it is working with Huawei Technologies to shift more training workloads onto domestic chips. Bloomberg and the Chinese financial magazine Caijing had reported on the latest round earlier.

Articles.Title: Chinese AI startup DeekSeek raises $15 billion ahead of potential IPO

stories.Headline: Former National Security Officials Warn Anthropic Ruling Threatens Federal AI Procurement
stories.Summary:
In October 2026, seventeen former senior national security officials asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to reconsider a ruling that upheld the Pentagon's decision to designate AI company Anthropic as a supply chain risk. Their court filing, dated Oct. 20, argues that the designation undermines national security and could discourage AI developers from adopting safety safeguards. The ruling they are challenging was a 2-1 decision that rejected Anthropic's challenge under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, which allows the government to address supply chain risks in federal procurement. The court said the Defense Department had "ample support" for concluding that continued use of Anthropic's Claude model by the department or its contractors posed a national security risk.

The dispute began when the Pentagon sought to use Claude for "all lawful uses," and Anthropic objected to two possible applications, mass surveillance and fully autonomous weapons. After negotiations broke down, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed that Anthropic be designated a supply chain risk, and he issued the formal determination on March 3, four days after publicly announcing the designation. The former officials argue that the Pentagon announced its decision before finishing the administrative review the law requires, so that the reasons were supplied afterward. They say a legitimate determination requires agencies to identify a specific threat, assess consequences, consider alternatives, and document their reasoning before acting. The officials also warn that the ruling could limit federal access to advanced AI as the United States competes with China, pointing to the Pentagon's interest in Anthropic's Claude Mythos model, which has advanced cybersecurity capabilities.

The filing is signed by former Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines, former national security advisers Jake Sullivan and Susan Rice, former Deputy Secretary of State Wendy Sherman, and former Homeland Security Under Secretary Suzanne Spaulding, among others. The officials, who served in both Republican and Democratic administrations, wrote that the Pentagon's action was politically motivated and that upholding it would let future administrations punish any company that falls out of favor. They also argue the Pentagon retaliated against Anthropic for its public positions on AI safety, citing Hegseth's criticism of the company's "sanctimonious rhetoric," "virtue-signaling," and "Silicon Valley ideology." The brief further notes that on Aug. 27 a federal district court in the Northern District of California granted Anthropic summary judgment on its First Amendment, due process, and Administrative Procedure Act challenges to the designation. The former officials are asking the full D.C. Circuit to rehear the case.

Articles.Title: Former National Security Officials Warn Anthropic Ruling Threatens Federal AI Procurement

stories.Headline: Billionaire Paul Tudor Jones warns AI and IPOs could hit stocks hard in 2027. Protect your nest egg now
stories.Summary:
Billionaire investor Paul Tudor Jones has warned that 2027 could be a very difficult year for the stock market. He made the remark on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on October 13, 2026, after AI-driven gains had fueled a broad market boom. His concern is that rising corporate fundraising for AI, along with large public listings, will put more shares up for sale and compete for investors' money. Jones said he plans to be short the market for the entire year.

The article explains that buybacks and acquisitions have historically removed shares from circulation, but that balance may shift as new offerings grow. Apple repurchased 402 million shares for $89.3 billion in fiscal 2025, while Microsoft's 2023 purchase of Activision Blizzard cancelled shareholder stock in exchange for $95 per share in cash. Jones also points to lockup expirations, which can release large blocks of stock for sale once restrictions end. He compared current conditions to 1999, describing a divide between businesses benefiting from AI and those being left behind. The article notes that his warning concerns what could follow rather than a forecast of an immediate collapse.

The warning comes from Jones himself, founder of Tudor Investment Corp., and the article presents it as his personal view rather than a settled outcome. The piece also stresses that a technology can succeed even if some investments tied to it fail, and that falling valuations can offset rising earnings. Jones expects some strength to remain possible before the end of 2026. The article suggests readers consider how much of their retirement savings depends on the market continuing to rise.

The article is a sponsored and promotional piece, and it includes advertisements for gold IRAs, rental property investing and financial advisor matching. It cites a World Gold Council survey in which 90% of respondents cited gold's crisis performance as a reason to hold it. It also notes that a portfolio starting at 60% stocks could drift to 80% after market gains if not rebalanced. The articles do not describe any regulatory action, and no further developments are reported beyond Jones's stated plan.

Articles.Title: Billionaire Paul Tudor Jones warns AI and IPOs could hit stocks hard in 2027. Protect your nest egg now

stories.Headline: A New AI Disclosure Law from Pennsylvania. But What Does It Actually Cover?
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, known as SB 806, which the Loeb & Loeb article describes as following similar laws in New York and California. The law's stated aim is transparency, but the article says its wording leaves open what actually triggers a disclosure. The law takes effect December 21, 2026, 60 days after signing. Under the enacted text, an advertiser must disclose AI use only when synthetic content is used in a way that creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin or authenticity of the advertised goods or services.

The article says this raises several questions, including what counts as false and whether a disclosure can cure a misleading ad. It also notes the law covers synthetic content generally, including images, video and audio that have been significantly modified or generated by AI, not only synthetic performers. The required disclosure must state that the content was modified or generated using artificial intelligence, be clear and conspicuous, appear the first time the content is shown, and be permanent where technically feasible. The law exempts evidently fictional content, parody, satire, commentary or criticism, and text-only content.

The article attributes the lead sponsorship to Sen. Nick Pisciottano, who said Pennsylvanians deserve to know whether an ad was created by a person or generated by AI. His broad description differs from the narrower standard the enacted text sets, and a co-sponsor described the aim as AI content that makes a product appear better than it is. When another senator objected that the bill does not say false compared to what, neither chamber changed the language. Enforcement rests only with the attorney general and district attorneys, who can seek an injunction or bring a civil action, with a possible fine of up to $3,000 plus attorney fees and costs, and there is no private right of action.

The authors frame the law as one that leaves advertisers to decide for themselves what triggers it, with little guidance or enforcement yet. They suggest enforcers may read it more broadly than its text, so many advertisers may add disclosures to AI-generated or AI-altered material rather than apply the test. The article also compares Pennsylvania with New York and California, noting Pennsylvania does not single out synthetic performers, has no knowledge requirement, and has no express exemption for expressive works or translations. The authors expect more states to follow with their own approaches.

Articles.Title: A New AI Disclosure Law from Pennsylvania. But What Does It Actually Cover? - Loeb & Loeb LLP

stories.Headline: Cal Poly reveals new NVIDIA powered AI Factory system for student research
stories.Summary:
Cal Poly San Luis Obispo unveiled a new NVIDIA-powered AI factory system on campus on October 22, during the school's AI Day event. The system is not a physical building but a computing setup that gives students and faculty access to powerful resources for AI projects too large or complex for standard computers. It is built on an NVIDIA DGX BasePOD system and carries a cost of $3 million. The reporting describes it as a way to lower the cost barriers to ambitious AI work while letting students learn new technology as it develops.

According to Cal Poly, hosting the system on campus gives the university more control over how its data is used and how the technology is developed. The system is designed to let students research and process very large volumes of information. The article presents the investment as a means of expanding hands-on access to advanced computing for student research. It does not describe any specific projects or results yet produced with the system.

Cal Poly announced the system during its AI Day, where the featured speaker was Charlie Wuischpard, NVIDIA's vice president of Americas Enterprise Sales. His appearance linked the campus launch to the chipmaker's enterprise business. The article does not report any remarks from him beyond his role at the event. It also does not say what comes next for the system or when students will begin using it.

Articles.Title: Cal Poly reveals new NVIDIA powered AI Factory system for student research

stories.Headline: As AI layoff fears mount, lawmakers weigh a bigger safety net for workers
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers in Washington are weighing a series of bills to protect American workers from job losses that artificial intelligence could cause. Their proposals vary in scope, though many focus on training programs for workers whose roles are eliminated. On a Friday in late October 2026, Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, a Democrat, backed a bill called The Stability and Opportunity for Workers Act. The measure would extend unemployment benefits during high-unemployment periods, and it would also provide education and retraining for higher-paying jobs to workers displaced by AI.

The Oregon senator's bill would extend unemployment benefits to 52 weeks once the unemployment rate reaches 8.5%, which is double the current standard of up to 26 weeks. Other proposals are more varied in their approach. Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona introduced the Make AI Work for Americans Act last month, which would create three excise taxes on the AI industry, including a 5% tax on digital advertising revenue, an AI usage tax and a 50% excess profits tax. Those revenues would go into a fund that could be used to retrain displaced workers. Representatives Greg Casar, Valerie Foushee and Sara Jacobs introduced the AI Tax and Work Protection Act in August, which would tax AI companies based on token usage at a rate that rises as unemployment rises.

The concerns behind these bills come from warnings by AI industry leaders and other prominent figures. Last year, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios that AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10% to 20% within one to five years. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates also warned in a recent essay that AI could put millions of jobs at risk. Economists note that those projections have not yet materialized, and that AI-related layoffs so far have mostly been concentrated in the tech industry. Still, a recent Associated Press-NORC poll found that nearly 80% of Americans said protecting workers in the age of AI is extremely or very important.

Another proposal, the AI-Related Job Impacts Clarity Act, is aimed at transparency rather than direct support. Senators Mark Warner of Virginia, a Democrat, and Josh Hawley of Missouri, a Republican, introduced it last year, and it would require major companies and federal agencies to report AI-related layoffs to the Department of Labor. The Labor Department would then make that data public. A House version was introduced in July by Representatives Steven Horsford of Nevada and Sara Jacobs of California, along with James Moylan, the delegate for Guam.

Articles.Title: As AI layoff fears mount, lawmakers weigh a bigger safety net for workers

stories.Headline: Reps. call on state Senate to pass bill to regulate use of AI in campaign advertisements
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania state representatives are calling on the state Senate to pass House Bill 811, legislation that would regulate the use of artificial intelligence in campaign advertisements. The reporting, published October 21, 2026, says the House already voted unanimously to pass the bill in June. Samantha Sobel reported the story for WHP in Harrisburg, and the coverage appeared on several local station websites that day. The push comes as lawmakers say AI-generated political deepfakes have become more common in campaigns.

The bill would require disclosure whenever AI is used in campaign ads and would set guidelines for how the technology may be used in them. It would also let candidates bring civil actions against individuals or entities that publish AI-generated content without the required disclosures. Penalties under the bill could reach $50,000. Officials say the legislation is meant to protect voters from being misled by fabricated statements attributed to candidates.

The primary sponsor is Representative Khan, who said candidates are now putting words in their opponents' mouths that they never said. Khan described the bill as bipartisan and said it has passed the House for two legislative sessions without any action in the Republican-controlled Senate. Khan also pointed to recent AI-generated attack ads as evidence of why the bill matters, while saying candidates are free to criticize opponents. Khan urged the Senate to act, saying the technology is already out in the open.

The articles do not say whether the Senate has scheduled any vote on the bill or what its leadership has said about it. The coverage describes the proposal as an effort to address a growing problem in election advertising, but it does not describe any specific ad that led to the bill. The articles also do not say whether similar measures are under consideration in other states. What happens next depends on whether the Senate takes up House Bill 811 in a future session.

Articles.Title: Reps. call on state Senate to pass bill to regulate use of AI in campaign advertisements - fox56.com

stories.Headline: Kansas Senate Rivals Clash Over Trump, AI Regulation, And Gender In Fiery Midterm Debate
stories.Summary:
Republican Senator Roger Marshall and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton clashed sharply during an hourlong Kansas Senate debate held on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, less than two weeks before Election Day. The two men argued over immigration, artificial intelligence, transgender athletes, and personal controversies. Marshall is seeking a second term, while Hamilton, a longtime pastor, is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932. The race has drawn heavy national attention as both parties fight for control of the Senate. President Donald Trump had traveled to Kansas earlier that week to campaign for Marshall.

The debate opened with both candidates confronted over separate controversies. Marshall was asked about a New York Times review finding that his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills, and he said the practice gave away $3 to $4 million in charity each year while also running a business with 300 employees. Hamilton was questioned about how he handled allegations that a volunteer at his church's summer camp had been accused of sexual abuse, and he acknowledged he should have acted more decisively. Moderators also played footage of Trump urging Kansas voters to treat the race as if he were on the ballot. Marshall was asked whether Trump's endorsement meant he backed the president's entire agenda, and he said he had objected to Trump several times, including over immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports.

On artificial intelligence, Hamilton called for sweeping federal oversight, comparing AI to nuclear weapons and arguing that the government should create an agency similar to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. When asked which specific rules he would support, he said he was not sure yet. Marshall favored a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, child protection, and privacy, and Hamilton pushed back by describing AI as a potential existential threat. On transgender participation in women's sports, Hamilton said eligibility decisions should generally be made locally while stating his personal opposition, and Marshall said boys and girls should compete in separate sports by high school and criticized national Democrats for what he called "transgender ideology." Both candidates agreed when asked that there are two genders.

The debate also highlighted the stakes of the contest and the candidates' efforts to define their positions. Marshall urged Trump voters to support him, warning that a Hamilton victory could hand Democrats control of the Senate, while acknowledging his disagreements with the president. Hamilton distanced himself from former President Joe Biden, calling Biden's border approach a disaster, and pledged not to support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader if Democrats win control. The articles do not report the results of the election, and the Kansas race remains one of the closely watched contests as the November midterms approach.

Articles.Title: Kansas Senate Rivals Clash Over Trump, AI Regulation, And Gender In Fiery Midterm Debate

stories.Headline: Hitachi Energy develops power system simulation with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help accelerate AI factory deployment
stories.Summary:
Hitachi Energy has announced a new simulation capability built on integrated NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, which lets data center teams test how future AI factory power systems might perform before they are built. The tool was announced in Berlin on October 23, 2026, and it joins the wider NVIDIA DSXSim partner ecosystem. It brings AI load scenarios and power system models into one shared digital environment. Teams can compare alternative designs, assess resilience, and reach more informed decisions earlier in planning.

Power infrastructure is a critical factor in how quickly and at what scale AI factories can be deployed. According to the article, electricity demand from data centers rose 17 percent in 2025, and consumption from AI-focused facilities grew faster still, well ahead of overall global demand growth. Operators must make key design choices that affect their ability to deliver with speed, reliability, scalability, and long-term resilience. The initial focus of the simulation is 800-volt direct current architectures, which are being developed to meet the rising power density and efficiency needs of next-generation AI factories. Grid-to-rack simulation can give insight into how such systems behave before they are deployed at scale.

The capability is part of a close collaboration between Hitachi Energy and NVIDIA on 800 VDC AI factories. Using OpenUSD-based workflows powered by NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, engineering data and Hitachi Energy power system models can be evaluated together in the shared environment. Marco Berardi, Head of Grid & Power Quality Solutions and Service at Hitachi Energy, said that as AI factories scale, access to electricity and the ability to deploy infrastructure quickly are becoming more important, and that combining Hitachi Energy's electrification expertise with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries lets customers explore and optimize power architectures before deployment. The development also follows the recent qualification of Hitachi Energy's battery energy storage system as NVIDIA DSX Ready BESS, which helps customers identify components that meet applicable NVIDIA DSX reference design requirements.

The article gives context on the companies involved. Hitachi Energy describes itself as a global leader in electrification, with an installed base in over 140 countries, around 56,000 employees in 60 countries, and revenues of around $20 billion USD. Hitachi, its parent group, reported revenues of 10,586.7 billion yen for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026. The article does not describe specific next steps or delivery timelines for the simulation capability.

Articles.Title: Hitachi Energy develops power system simulation with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help accelerate AI factory deployment

stories.Headline: Crusoe: Building AI Factories at a US$30.9bn Valuation
stories.Summary:
Crusoe, an AI infrastructure company, raised US$3.9bn in a Series F round in September 2026 at a post-money valuation of US$30.9bn. The article reports that the company now has more than US$140bn in total contracted value and over 6GW of gross contracted capacity, with about 1GW delivered and operational. Its best-known project is a campus in Abilene, Texas, where OpenAI trained its model Astra, and Crusoe designed and built the site. The company was founded on using wasted natural gas to power computing and has since grown into a major builder of AI infrastructure.

The company's strategy is vertical integration, meaning it controls every stage from power supply to the rental of computing capacity through Crusoe Cloud. In practice, it secures energy, designs and builds data centre campuses, manufactures some of its own equipment, and sells compute to customers. Its energy deals span grid, battery, nuclear, thermal and renewable sources. The Armstrong County campus near Amarillo, being built for Google, connects directly to two adjacent 265.5MW wind farms. Aalo Atomics has a partnership aimed at delivering the first nuclear-powered AI factory in 2027, and ON.energy will supply 5GW of AI UPS systems across several hyperscale campuses.

Chase Lochmiller, Crusoe's co-founder and CEO, has described the strategy as controlling the infrastructure from electrons to tokens. The article attributes the company's growth in cloud business to bookings that are up more than 20 times year on year in 2026 so far. Its Managed Inference product has passed US$100m in contracted annual recurring revenue within a year of launch. Perplexity signed a multi-year deal in September 2026 for dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 clusers, and Thinking Machines Lab agreed a US$65m-a-year contract for open-model inference days later.

The Series F was co-led by Atreides Management, Mubadala Capital and Valor Equity Partners, and the funds are intended for the next wave of campuses and cloud capacity. Crusoe now employs more than 1,800 people across five countries and has added board members including Cloudflare CFO Thomas Seifert. In October 2026 it pledged US$50m in compute credits to the White House AI Science Initiative. The article does not describe any specific regulatory or market challenges facing the company.

Articles.Title: Crusoe: Building AI Factories at a US$30.9bn Valuation - AI Magazine

stories.Headline: How Investors Are Reacting To Kyndryl Holdings (KD) AI Deal With Toyota Finance
stories.Summary:
Toyota Finance Corporation recently announced that Kyndryl Holdings and Toyota Systems are applying Kyndryl’s Agentic AI Framework to overhaul Toyota Finance’s IT service operations. The work covers infrastructure design, change management, impact analysis, and AI agent based review workflows across production environments. The announcement was reported on October 20, 2026. Kyndryl also received recognition as a Leader in IDC’s global digital workplace services assessment.

The Toyota Finance deployment fits into Kyndryl’s effort to shift from legacy, pre-spin contracts toward newer, AI and cloud heavy work. The company’s narrative projects US$15.2 billion in revenue and US$472.5 million in earnings by 2029, assuming flat revenue trends and an earnings increase of about US$274.5 million from US$198.0 million today. Revenue is forecast to edge down about 0.4 percent a year, and margins sit at 0.6 percent. Kyndryl last closed at $13.89, slightly below a widely followed fair value estimate of $14.10 that applies a 12.46 percent discount rate.

The lowest analysts worry AI projects stay stuck in pilots, so revenue drifts about 2 percent lower each year and earnings only reach around US$433.2 million by 2029. Kyndryl’s share price has bounced sharply, with a 1-day return of 4.59 percent, a 7-day return of 13.48 percent, and a 30-day return of 15.08 percent. However, total shareholder return over the past year has declined 51.52 percent, and the 5-year total shareholder return is down 60.87 percent. The market is charging a price-to-earnings ratio of 34.8 times, which is richer than the US IT industry at 22.9 times.

The near term swing factor is execution on renewals and new signings as older contracts roll off. Complex account transitions, debt coverage pressures, and weaker margins limit how much benefit investors actually see from efficiency projects. If agentic AI engagements become more common, they could support higher margin contracts, stronger earnings growth, and more stable free cash flow. Kyndryl is also expanding AI, data, and cybersecurity services through investments in Kyndryl Bridge and alliances such as Databricks.

Articles.Title: How Investors Are Reacting To BigBear.ai Holdings (BBAI) $225 Million Contract Wins - Simply Wall Street
