stories.Headline: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend
stories.Summary:
Block, the payments company led by Jack Dorsey, has announced an AI model called Dessa that it says was trained "from scratch on nothing but human conversation." To show what it can do, the company shared chat exchanges with people that are sometimes natural and sometimes a little awkward or uncanny. In one example shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam, the model briefly mistakes the speaker for someone named "Ronaldo" before the conversation settles into a mostly natural back and forth. The article was published on October 23, 2026.

The Dessa website describes the model as a true speech-to-speech system whose knowledge came entirely from human speech, and it says the model can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max or better. Other examples on the site include a discussion of Christopher Nolan's films that drifts into an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer's Superman films, and a conversation in which the model responds to news of a surprise trip to Paris with what the site describes as teary gratitude. A clip also pits Dessa against OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model, and the article says Dessa comes across as more natural in that exchange. The article notes that the clips can be heard in an accompanying video.

The Dessa team gives three reasons for building the model: curiosity, better understanding between humans and AI, and safety. On safety, the team argues that current voice AI flattens speech into text and cannot respond to emotion in people's voices, which it describes as a problem as AI gains power and independence. The team says it will give "a small group of AI safety researchers" early access to the model. The articles do not say when broader access will be available or whether Block plans a public release.

Articles.Title: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend

stories.Headline: DOE’s Bridget Carper Arnone: Trust Is the Foundation for AI at Scale
stories.Summary:
Bridget Carper Arnone, the Department of Energy's deputy chief information officer, has said that trust and cybersecurity must come before artificial intelligence can scale across the department. In an interview with MeriTalk published October 22, 2026, she explained that DOE's fiscal year 2027 technology priorities rank cybersecurity and risk management first, followed by data management and analytics, then AI and machine learning. Arnone said employees will not put their data into tools they do not trust, so adoption depends on resilience. She described AI as a multiplier that only works once the underlying data is reliable and accessible to the right users.

Arnone also described how the department's generative AI suite, Joulix, grew after leadership changed the conversation. The platform began rolling out at the end of 2023 with about 1,000 users, even though it had security authorization. Adoption rose after undersecretaries, office leaders, and component CIOs told employees they supported the tool and were using it themselves. Joulix now has roughly 22,000 users, and the team behind it received a Secretary of Energy Achievement Award. Arnone said the lesson is that leaders must actively give people permission to change how they work.

Arnone said DOE is now exploring AI agents to take over repeatable workflows, such as technology onboarding, so employees can focus on quality control and judgment. The department is working with its cybersecurity leaders on how to secure agents and manage several of them within one environment. Security staff now join technology and customer discussions early, so protections are built alongside a capability rather than added after testing. Arnone also questioned whether repeated reviews of already controlled tools reduce risk as much as reviewing genuinely new models or threats would.

Arnone said budgets will not grow, so agencies must stop low-value work instead of only starting new initiatives. She urged leaders to ask who still uses older systems, what value they produce, and whether they can be consolidated or retired. She said success should be measured by adoption and mission results, such as reduced administrative burden, faster work, stronger collaboration, and more scientific discovery, rather than by how many tools are available. The article does not describe specific deadlines for decommissioning systems or launching agent deployments.

Articles.Title: DOE’s Bridget Carper Arnone: Trust Is the Foundation for AI at Scale - MeriTalk

stories.Headline: Turmoil hits AI build-out as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
stories.Summary:
Investor concern about the artificial intelligence build-out pushed markets lower this week, with neocloud providers taking some of the steepest losses. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN each fell sharply and were down well over 30% for October, while CoreWeave's credit default swap spreads widened past 11%, a level generally seen as distress. Yields on CoreWeave's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes topped 15%. Elsewhere, Elice Group in South Korea fell 30% in its market debut on Tuesday, and Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after cutting its annual earnings forecast.

On Thursday, SK Hynix said it was withdrawing its planned initial public offering for Solidigm, its U.S.-based unit that makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers. The company cited market volatility and recent share price trends in its release, and said the IPO had been expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns. Meta's stock fell 7% on Thursday after it reported negative free cash flow of over $2 billion in the third quarter and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditure to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on leases and contracts, with more than $450 billion of that in non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements.

Credit markets reflected the strain. Meta's five-year credit default swap spreads reached all-time highs above 124 basis points, while spreads on Nvidia and Oracle also hit records at 126 and 343 basis points this week. Oracle's stock has lost more than a third of its value this year, and the company faces the risk of a credit rating downgrade. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, speaking at a conference in Berlin, said demand for neoclouds is "off the charts" and that the demand for capital exceeds its availability, a shortage he expects will be resolved. Analysts at Gartner, meanwhile, predict that 80% of neocloud companies will either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.

Market participants are watching how the trade plays out, and investors are increasingly looking for ways to hedge their exposure. John Williams of law firm Milbank LLP said the scale of spending makes risk management tools appropriate regardless of whether an investor is bullish or bearish. Portfolio manager Brian Stutland of Equity Armor Investments said the pressures are interconnected and voiced concern that the strain could spread to the broader Nasdaq. Alphabet, which reports third-quarter earnings next week along with Microsoft and Amazon, had been the worst performer among the hyperscalers, with its shares falling 6% ahead of that report.

Articles.Title: Turmoil hits AI build-out as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO

stories.Headline: No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector
stories.Summary:
Apollo Global Management published an analysis on October 24, 2026, arguing that artificial intelligence has so far produced no financial payoff for American companies outside the technology sector. The piece, written under the Apollo Chief Economist's research, compares the so-called Mag 7 technology firms with the rest of the S&P 500, which it calls the S&P 493. It reports that revenue per worker and profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but remain flat for the S&P 493, and that there are still no signs of AI lifting productivity growth. Apollo's view is that mainstream firms are beginning to treat spending on AI tokens as a cost that weighs on margins rather than as a source of growth.

The article also says that venture-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but that mainstream corporate America does not appear to need the latest models or to be willing to pay for them. It concludes that while agentic AI and token spending remain confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited. The authors frame the coming test as whether ordinary businesses can turn increasingly cheap, commoditized intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins. They argue this may be harder than it sounds, since business intelligence depends largely on judgment, which varies with context.

Apollo's analysts say that AI does not grasp accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue and margins. Apollo's Chief Economist, Torsten Slok, is named as the source of the research, and the document cites data from Bloomberg, Macrobond, the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco and the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. The firm adds that its opinions are the current judgment of the speaker, may change without notice, and do not necessarily reflect the views of Apollo as a whole. The bottom line, in the article's words, is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493 rather than the Mag 7, and that so far there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside technology.

Articles.Title: No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector

stories.Headline: Aging US paper mills set for AI-driven transformation led by ORNL
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Energy has launched a national initiative called the Center for Research and Advancement of Forest Product Technologies, known as CRAFT, to modernize the country's pulp, paper, and packaging industry. The center is led by the department's Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which is bringing together several national laboratories, universities, and industry partners. The initiative was reported on October 23, 2026, and it aims to help domestic producers stay competitive while the sector continues to depend on aging mill equipment. The industry supports thousands of manufacturing jobs, and its infrastructure is in many cases decades old.

Rather than building new mills, CRAFT will focus on getting more value from existing facilities through digital methods. Researchers plan to use artificial intelligence, automation, complex modeling, and data analysis to find operational bottlenecks, reduce downtime, improve yields, and lower production costs. The program will also target some of the most energy-intensive stages of production, including next-generation pulping, chemical recovery, dewatering, and drying. These steps account for a significant share of production costs, so they offer room for efficiency gains. The center will combine molecular-scale modeling with AI-enabled discovery and experimental testing to speed the path from lab work to factory use.

Daniel Coughlin, executive director of CRAFT and a senior research and development staff member at Oak Ridge, said the industry is vital to rural communities, noting that much of its infrastructure is decades old. The center is funded by the Industrial Technologies Office within the Department of Energy's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation. It is supported by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Idaho National Laboratory, and the newly established National Laboratory of the Rockies, along with a network of industrial partners. Gregg Beckham, senior research fellow and the National Laboratory of the Rockies lead for CRAFT, is quoted describing the effort as a way to bridge the gap between laboratory research and factory deployment.

In its first phase, CRAFT will work directly with manufacturers to identify operating problems and decide which pilot-scale technologies should be tested before commercial rollout. The center also plans to give companies access to advanced automation, simulation, and data-analysis tools that many traditional mills lack. Art Ragauskas, chief technology officer for CRAFT, said the center should reduce the technical and financial risks of adopting new technologies. Beyond research, CRAFT is intended to act as a national hub that brings together manufacturers, equipment suppliers, downstream customers, and researchers. Department officials said the goal is to strengthen domestic manufacturing and sustain high-value jobs in rural communities.

Articles.Title: Aging US paper mills set for AI-driven transformation led by ORNL - Interesting Engineering

stories.Headline: AI devours a fifth of companies’ IT budgets
stories.Summary:
According to a new study by the research firm Forrester, AI will account for 20% of corporate technology spending in 2027. At the same time, more than half of IT executives are expected to miss their return-on-investment targets. The findings were reported by The Register and originally appeared in Computer Sweden. The study points to a gap between the money companies are putting into AI and the results they are getting back from it.

In the survey, 45% of AI decision-makers said investments must produce a positive return within one year to be considered successful. Only 22% reported a positive effect on their company's operating profit over the past year. Forrester attributes part of the problem to companies buying AI technology without also changing their organizations and work processes. As a result, financial gains tend to show up only within individual use cases rather than across the business.

Forrester expects companies to increasingly turn to open AI models in the future, since they are cheaper to run. More expensive and advanced models are expected to be kept for more critical tasks. Together, these shifts are presented as ways to keep AI costs under control. The articles provide no further figures on how quickly this change is expected to happen.

Articles.Title: AI devours a fifth of companies’ IT budgets

stories.Headline: Redmond-based startup develops new robot weeder using AI technology
stories.Summary:
A Redmond-based startup called Aigen has developed a solar-powered robot weeder that uses AI to tell weeds apart from crops, according to a report published by KUOW on October 23, 2026. The machine, known as the Element Gen 2, looks like a drafting table on wheels and has a solar panel on its top surface that powers it. Four metal arms underneath pluck weeds and fling them behind the machine as it rolls through a farm plot. The company's cofounder, Richard Wurden, said the aim was to control weeds without diesel or chemical sprays.

Conventional weeding of low-cost crops often relies on herbicides, the article explains, and that approach has drawbacks. Rui Liu, an assistant professor of weed science at Washington State University, is quoted saying that repeated herbicide use can produce resistant weed strains, which makes the chemicals less effective over time. Liu added that growers need diverse management strategies to keep weeds under control in the long term. The Aigen founders said their interest in non-toxic weed control was personal, since Wurden has Type 1 diabetes and cofounder Kenny Lee has non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and both conditions have been linked to pesticide use.

Wurden said the company chose solar power so the machine would not need refueling, which he described as making it truly autonomous, in contrast to equipment that has to be trucked out and filled. The article notes that rising fuel prices have brought the company more than 30 orders for its solar-powered models. Aigen is not the only startup working on farm technology, as the report points out that Seattle-based Carbon Robotics uses AI detection and laser weeding. The article also observes that many companies still depend on diesel to run their equipment.

Articles.Title: Redmond-based startup develops new robot weeder using AI technology

stories.Headline: Councilors seek to draw hard lines around the use of AI by City Hall, but the borders are already blurred - Cambridge | Somerville Independent
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, the Somerville City Council held a meeting where artificial intelligence came up repeatedly, including the adoption of a law setting boundaries for its use in government. The councilors also passed a resolution calling for commonsense policies on AI in creating media and in staffing City Hall. The law and civil rights orders were sent to the council's Legislative Matters Committee for closer review. The article describes the discussion as one that showed keeping AI out of government work, or even defining what that includes, will not be simple.

The proposed ordinance says city departments cannot use AI in law enforcement actions such as arrests, searches and investigations. At a committee meeting on Tuesday, however, city staff reported that Somerville uses only one true AI product, and it is for police. That software, called Blue Voice, was created by David Lawrence, and it summarizes laws, policies and procedures to advise officers. David Slonina, the city's deputy director of information technology, said it is a closed-loop system trained only on Somerville policies and transmits no data. Slonina also said other AI use is incidental to software, such as email sorting, traffic lights and virus protection.

Councilor Jon Link, who introduced the motion, said the law does not bar the city from using AI but requires that its biases and flaws be understood. He gave examples of appropriate uses, such as formatting an Excel document, and inappropriate ones, such as deciding where a library branch might go or whether a community member goes to prison. The law would also require content made mostly by AI to be labeled and an annual report on how much AI the city uses and how. Councilor Will Mbah said AI use must be transparent, accountable and consistent with civil rights and privacy protections, and that residents should know when it materially influences decisions about housing, benefits or employment. Councilor JT Scott noted that police and other departments have already used AI for graphics and work materials.

Councilor Ben Wheeler said the matters are in good enough shape to open to close review by the administration, the public, the council and advocacy groups, and that the guiding goal is clarity about the limited requirements and the high-risk cases they cover. The resolution passed by the council, led by Link with Scott and councilor Naima Sait, is simpler, calling for policies that favor human creative work and prohibit using AI to replace workers. Link said the city should use artists rather than AI for public materials and should not use AI to eliminate positions. The article does not say when the committee will take up the proposals.

Articles.Title: Councilors seek to draw hard lines around the use of AI by City Hall, but the borders are already blurred - Cambridge | Somerville Independent -

stories.Headline: Kansas State hosting Heartland AI Symposium
stories.Summary:
The Heartland AI Symposium, titled "Our Society in the Age of AI," is set to take place November 10 to 12 at Kansas State University, according to a report published by WIBW on October 23, 2026. The event is described as a wide-ranging discussion that has grown over four years from an initial exploration of what artificial intelligence is to a broader look at what it can do. A free townhall discussion will open the event from 6:30 to 8 p.m. on November 10 at the Manhattan Public Library. The main symposium sessions are held at the K-State Student Union.

Attendance costs $150 in person and $125 online, with discounts available for students, educators and K-State staff. The agenda covers topics including education, language, security and ethics. Full agenda and registration details are posted at k-state.edu/ai-symposium. Those interested are directed to that site for the complete schedule and sign-up information. Raelynne Hale, a professor of modern languages at K-State, serves as the symposium director.

She described the scope of the agenda in an interview on Eye on NE Kansas, the WIBW program that previewed the event. The article reports her remarks as an overview of the topics planned for the three days. It does not give further detail on specific speakers or sessions. The article does not describe any changes or new requirements tied to the event beyond the registration and attendance details already noted. It also does not state any outcomes or follow-up plans for the symposium.

Articles.Title: Kansas State hosting Heartland AI Symposium

stories.Headline: AI in Higher Education Internal Audit: 2026 Survey Results
stories.Summary:
A 2026 survey of higher education internal audit leaders, run by EisnerAmper with the Association of College and University Auditors (ACUA), found that AI use in these offices is moving faster than the governance around it. The survey was facilitated for participating ACUA institutions through a 34-question instrument, and the results were published on October 23, 2026. Of the institutions that responded, 34 were counted in the findings. Respondents pointed to data quality and staff AI literacy as the main barriers to broader adoption, while only 3% named leadership buy-in as their primary obstacle.

Internal audit teams are using AI mainly for writing and planning work. Seventy-one percent use it to write and edit audit reports, 68% use it for risk assessments and audit planning, and 68% use it for regulatory and policy research. Far fewer use it for analytical work, with 35% applying it to data analysis and continuous monitoring and fewer than 9% using it to review contracts and vendor agreements. The authors suggest teams worry about accuracy and security because contracts hold sensitive information, and they recommend starting any such work in a secure, institution-approved environment with human verification of the results.

Governance is lagging behind use. Only 12 of the 34 responding institutions have a formal AI policy or guidelines, and half are still developing one. Technology leaders own AI governance at 44% of institutions, while 24% report no single owner or structure. None of the responding internal audit leaders lead or co-lead governance, and 62% are only informed of it or not involved. The authors also note that 41% of institutions have a policy on students' use of generative AI, even though 65% of respondents cite academic integrity as a significant concern.

Respondents rated nine AI risk categories on a one-to-five scale. The highest concerns were cybersecurity risks from AI and over-reliance on unvetted AI output, each rated four or five by 76% of respondents. Data privacy and FERPA compliance came next at 74%, with 56% giving it the top rating of five. Building team AI literacy and skills is the top priority for the next 12 to 18 months, and four respondents, or 12%, said AI is not a current priority. The article recommends three starting steps: building an AI inventory with IT and procurement, placing AI auditing in both the skills plan and the audit plan, and documenting how AI-assisted work is verified before it reaches a report.

Articles.Title: AI in Higher Education Internal Audit: 2026 Survey Results

stories.Headline: AG warns Colom to pull A.I. ads or face injunction, though argument raises questions - the mississippi independent
stories.Summary:
Attorney General Lynn Fitch warned Scott Colom and his U.S. Senate campaign on October 23, 2026, that artificial intelligence ads they posted to social media appear to violate Mississippi's deepfake law and should be taken down. Her office said that if the ads stayed up, it could seek a court injunction. Colom said afterward that he would delete the postings because he did not want the attorney general to spend taxpayer money on litigation. Fitch also asked his campaign to preserve all records related to the matter. The statute Fitch cited is Section 97-13-47 of the state code, which took effect in 2024.

Under it, a violation carries up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine where the intent is to deter voting, and up to one year and $5,000 otherwise. The notice stopped short of a legal conclusion and said only that the ads "appear to violate" the law. Nothing had been filed in court as of the notice. The Mississippi Republican Party had asked Fitch to act in a seven-page letter sent on October 22 by party chair Mike Hurst. The complaint concerns a 19-second video posted on Facebook and Instagram on October 1 that shows a woman made to resemble Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith hurrying away from reporters into a car, with a narrator calling her "Cindy."

Both posts were captioned "Based on a true story" and did not say artificial intelligence was used. The video refers to a September 23 hallway exchange in which a correspondent for "The Don Lemon Show" approached Hyde-Smith, and Hurst's letter says she declined interviews and asked Capitol police to intervene. The law bars circulating a digitally fabricated depiction of a person within 90 days of an election without consent, but it does not apply to satire or parody. Hurst argued the video was not parody because it lacks humor, and he quoted Colom saying on October 16 that he was portraying a true story. Colom responded that the video was parody meant to highlight Hyde-Smith's avoidance of reporters.

Mississippi does not require political ads to disclose artificial intelligence use. State Senator Bradford Blackmon filed bills to require such disclosure, and the Senate passed the second version 52 to 0 on February 10, 2026, before it died in a House committee on March 3. The state also has an older campaign-speech law, Section 23-15-875, which the article notes was reenacted and amended over the years, while the U.S. Supreme Court's 1964 New York Times v. Sullivan decision requires public officials suing over criticism to prove falsity and reckless disregard for the truth. Election Day is November 3.

Articles.Title: AG warns Colom to pull A.I. ads or face injunction, though argument raises questions - the mississippi independent

stories.Headline: Chip Shares Slide as AI Spending Fears Outweigh Solidigm IPO Halt
stories.Summary:
Shares of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix fell in early trading on October 23, 2026, after a sharp drop in U.S. technology stocks the previous day. Samsung traded at 208,250 won, down 2.91 percent and below the 210,000-won level, while SK hynix slipped to 1,199,000 won, below the 1.2 million-won mark. The Kospi opened at 5,403.17, down 130.60 points or 2.36 percent, and the Kosdaq began at 748.32, down 2.07 percent. The decline followed a Nasdaq Composite drop of 2.60 percent on October 22, its steepest since June.

SK hynix said in a regulatory filing before the market opened that it was halting its review of a pre-IPO funding round and an initial public offering for Solidigm, its U.S. subsidiary. The company said it had examined several funding options to expand production capacity and strengthen competitiveness, but made the decision after weighing capital market conditions. It also said Solidigm's growth potential and investment needs had not changed, but that it had to reassess whether an IPO at this time was the most advantageous option for the company and its shareholders. Analyst Han Ji-young of Kiwoom Securities said the halt was likely to help improve sentiment toward chip stocks.

The main pressure came from renewed doubts about AI spending costs in U.S. markets. Meta reported third-quarter results that beat expectations but said it planned to issue a new class of non-voting shares to fund AI investment, and it raised the lower end of its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to $135 billion from $130 billion. Its third-quarter free cash flow came in at negative $2.12 billion, its first deficit since going public, and its shares fell about 7 percent. Nvidia and Micron also dropped, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 6.72 percent, while Brent crude rising above $113 a barrel over Middle East tensions added to the unease.

Analysts remain divided on the outlook. NH Investment & Securities projected the Kospi's range for the following week at 5,100 to 6,400, citing third-quarter corporate earnings and shareholder return policies as upside factors and geopolitical risk as a downside factor. Kiwoom's Han said domestic stocks could absorb early panic selling and recover some losses during the session. The articles do not report how the market closed that day beyond the later related headlines, which indicate a rebound in the Kospi after SK hynix's announcement.

Articles.Title: Chip Shares Slide as AI Spending Fears Outweigh Solidigm IPO Halt - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: A Starting Point for Your City’s AI Policy
stories.Summary:
The League of Minnesota Cities published a model artificial intelligence policy on October 23, 2026, to help cities use AI responsibly in their operations. The League says AI tools can save time and improve efficiency, but they also raise questions about data privacy, accuracy, and accountability. The guidance is aimed at cities whose staff use AI to draft communications, analyze information, or handle everyday tasks. It notes that cities need clear expectations for what the technology can and cannot be used for. The article explains why a policy matters, pointing to several risks.

Information entered into AI platforms may be retained by third-party providers, and automated recommendations can reflect errors and biases. The article also says cities have legal duties, including compliance with the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act, and that government data created with AI assistance is likely covered by those requirements. Without guidelines, employees may expose sensitive information or rely on content that has not been properly reviewed. A clear policy helps staff know when AI is useful and what precautions to take.

The League's model policy offers a framework that cities can adapt to their own operations, technology, and needs. It includes two options for permitted and prohibited uses and defines low-, moderate-, and high-risk data with precautions for each. It keeps employees responsible for reviewing, verifying, and approving AI-generated content and decisions, and it gives guidance on disclosing when AI has materially helped create documents or public communications. The article says cities should review and adapt the model with their city attorney before adopting it.

It also recommends regular reviews, since the technology continues to change. The League directs cities to a companion resource, Cities and Artificial Intelligence (AI): What You Should Know, which covers data classification, compliance with the Government Data Practices Act, and the risks of relying on AI-generated information. The article also lists the League's Resource Research Department, which can be reached through an online form or by phone at (651) 281-1200 or (800) 925-1122, to help cities with questions. The article closes by saying that AI may change how cities carry out their work but does not change their duty to protect government data and serve their communities.

Articles.Title: A Starting Point for Your City’s AI Policy

stories.Headline: Korean Animation Group Expands AI Ties With China at Shanghai Summit
stories.Summary:
Korea Animation Industry Association announced on October 23, 2026 that it had co-hosted the 2026 Yangtze River Delta Animation Industry Summit in Shanghai the previous day, October 22. The event was organized alongside the Shanghai Animation and Comic Industry Association and the Beijing Business Center of the Korea Creative Content Agency. Officials from both governments, along with platforms and studios such as ByteDance and iQIYI, took part in the gathering. The summit focused on AI-driven animation production and the joint creation of intellectual property between Korean and Chinese firms. At the summit, the organizations officially launched the Korea-China AIGC Creative Contest, which aims to build skills in AI-based content production and identify joint projects between creators in the two countries.

The Korea-China AI Exchange Association also joined discussions on AI video production technology and ways to link distribution through over-the-top services. Korean studios Studio Animal, Stellain and Ocon described their use of AI, their IP-focused strategies for global audiences, and their plans for growth alongside the AI industry. Roundtables and business networking sessions that followed covered co-production, IP licensing, investment and distribution cooperation. The articles give no figures for prize money, participant counts or deal values. Cho Kyung-hoon, chairman of the Korea Animation Industry Association, said that both industries can advance when Korea's original planning capabilities and adaptability combine with China's large market and industrial infrastructure.

He expressed hope that, starting with this summit, the two countries would move beyond simple exchanges to become practical partners pursuing the global market together. The association framed the event as a step toward deeper collaboration rather than a finished agreement. The articles do not describe any binding commitments made at the summit. The report places the summit within a broader push by Korean and Chinese content companies to use AI in production and to expand IP-based business. The articles do not say what follow-up events, contest timelines or joint projects are scheduled.

Articles.Title: Korean Animation Group Expands AI Ties With China at Shanghai Summit - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Nvidia lines up six suppliers to expand substrate, packaging, and testing capacity
stories.Summary:
Nvidia said on October 21, 2026, that it is working with six supply chain partners to expand manufacturing capacity in several parts of its production chain. The company named four areas where capacity is being added: substrates, advanced packaging, testing, and optical engines. The expansion is meant to meet growing demand for its accelerated computing and AI factory platforms. The report was published by DIGITIMES on October 22, 2026, and the announcement itself came the day before.

The articles provide no further figures, dates, or names for the six suppliers, and they do not specify how much capacity will be added or over what timeframe. What they do establish is the direction of the move, which is that Nvidia is bringing more outside manufacturers into the process of building the hardware behind its AI systems. The four areas named cover the steps that sit between chip design and finished products. Because the report is brief, it offers little detail on how the new arrangements will be structured.

The articles attribute the announcement to Nvidia itself, which described the partnerships as a way to support its accelerated computing and AI factory offerings. Beyond that statement, the report does not include comments from the suppliers or from any independent analysts. The text on the page is largely navigation and subscription material, so no additional remarks from the company are available in the source material. The article therefore rests on Nvidia's own description of its plans.

The surrounding coverage on the same site points to a broader industry context of tight packaging and foundry capacity. Other stories listed alongside this one discuss advanced packaging expansion and chipmaker pricing for 2027, though the articles do not connect those developments directly to Nvidia's announcement. The source material does not say what the next steps will be or when more details on the six suppliers will be released. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nvidia lines up six suppliers to expand substrate, packaging, and testing capacity - digitimes

stories.Headline: California To Require Human Corroboration of AI-Driven Discipline and Termination - Atkinson, Andelson, Loya, Ruud & Romo
stories.Summary:
California will soon bar employers from relying solely on automated decision systems when disciplining or firing workers. Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 947 into law on September 30, 2026, and it takes effect on July 1, 2027. The law does not ban employers from using AI tools in employment decisions. It does require that when an employer primarily relies on an automated system's output to discipline or terminate someone, a human must corroborate that output. Corroborating material can include supervisor evaluations, personnel files, work product, peer reviews, witness interviews, and relevant online customer reviews.

If the output cannot be corroborated, or a reviewer finds it inaccurate, incomplete, or misleading, the employer may not use it for that decision. The employer must also give the employee a plain-language written notice saying the decision primarily relied on an automated system and that a human reviewed it. The notice must include contact information for a human and explain the employee's right to a description of their own data used by the system. On request, the employer must provide that description in a form that anonymizes other people's personal information. The statute does not set a percentage or weighting test for when reliance counts as primary, which the author warns leaves employers without a safe harbor.

The article, written by Nicholas T. Spencer, a senior associate at the firm Atkinson, Andelson, Loya, Ruud & Romo, explains the law's terms and does not attribute any statement to the governor or legislators beyond the signing. It notes that the Labor Commissioner and public prosecutors will enforce the law, with civil penalties of $500 per violation. In superior court actions, a petitioner may seek temporary or preliminary injunctive relief, punitive damages, and attorney's fees and costs. The statute also prohibits using automated systems to violate employment or civil rights laws, to infer protected status under the Fair Employment and Housing Act, or to take adverse action against workers for exercising legal rights.

The author recommends that employers inventory every automated tool that informs discipline or termination, including performance dashboards, productivity analytics, attendance systems, and scoring built into HR platforms. Employers should prepare for human review of those decisions and develop a template notice to deliver when a decision is communicated. Supervisors and HR managers should also learn the new requirements before the effective date. The article presents these steps as practical preparation rather than as obligations the statute imposes beyond what is described above.

The expansion brings a semiconductor project into the region's development plans and concentrates it on the packaging stage that links chips to the systems that use them. Advanced packaging has become a bottleneck in AI hardware production, so added capacity of this kind is aimed at meeting that demand. The reporting frames the investment as a tripling of what Amkor had previously planned for the site. stories.Headline: Micron's vHBM Stacks DRAM on Top of the Processor, With Heat Dissipation the Biggest Hurdle and Mass Production Not Until 2028
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology has outlined a new memory design called vertical high-bandwidth memory, or vHBM, which stacks DRAM directly on top of the processor to shorten the data path and raise bandwidth for AI inference workloads. The company also described a second architecture, vertical edge inference memory, or vEIM, and a jump in its NAND roadmap. These plans were laid out at a technology and product webinar, and the articles place the new designs on a medium- to long-term timeline rather than in current products. The stacking approach creates a physical problem, because placing memory above the compute chip blocks the space the processor needs to shed heat. According to the articles, vHBM is targeted for mass production in 2028, with three product generations by 2030, while conventional HBM continues on its own path, with HBM4 having entered mass production in March 2026 and HBM4E sampling to major customers.

The vEIM design, which stacks low-power LPDDR memory on logic chips in edge devices, aims for bandwidth of 2TB per second and energy use below 1 picojoule per bit, with mass production also slated for 2028. On storage, Micron will move from ninth-generation NAND straight to the eleventh generation, skipping the tenth, and G11 is expected to enter mass production in the second half of next year. Karl Ackerman, a senior analyst at BNP Paribas, flagged the heat trade-off in a new research report and said it will limit where vHBM can be deployed. He expects vHBM to coexist with conventional HBM rather than replace it, with system vendors choosing designs based on bandwidth needs, thermal limits and packaging complexity. Micron President and Chief Technology and Product Officer Scott DeBoer described the NAND jump as a significant leap and said the engineering team revisited the memory to better serve future AI products.

He also said high-bandwidth NAND will sit closer to the compute rather than at the edge of accelerators, which he said does not make sense. The articles present these designs as a longer-term opportunity rather than a driver of near-term results. Ackerman believes Micron's current earnings still rest mainly on high-bandwidth memory, server DRAM, enterprise SSDs and tight supply, which the company expects to persist for at least another two years. The main questions ahead are whether Micron can turn these architectures into products customers adopt, and whether it can handle the thermal and manufacturing challenges that come with stacking.

Articles.Title: Micron's vHBM Stacks DRAM on Top of the Processor, With Heat Dissipation the Biggest Hurdle and Mass Production Not Until 2028 - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: TSMC advances CoPoS packaging at Taoyuan Longtan site
stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: AI Memory Boom Is Funding China's Chip Catch-Up
stories.Summary:
Chinese memory chipmakers are closing the gap with their Korean rivals, and industry watchers say the AI memory boom is paying for it. According to a Seoul Economic Daily report published on October 23, 2026, ChangXin Memory Technologies, a Chinese DRAM maker, and Yangtze Memory Technologies, a NAND flash producer, are expanding capacity and moving into each other's main business lines. The report says CXMT is pursuing NAND research while YMTC has started work on DRAM, suggesting both want to become full-line suppliers. The article's author is Seo Jong-gap, and industry watchers quoted in the piece say competition could intensify sharply once China's new fabs reach full operation in 2027 and 2028.

The growth figures are steep. CXMT's preliminary nine-month guidance, released on October 16, implies third-quarter revenue of 114.7 billion to 119.7 billion yuan, roughly seven times the year-earlier figure. Counterpoint Research put CXMT's share of global DRAM revenue at 10 percent in the second quarter, up from 4 percent a year earlier. SemiAnalysis projects CXMT's monthly DRAM wafer capacity will rise from about 350,000 wafers at the end of this year to 500,000 by the end of 2028. YMTC has reached third place globally in NAND shipment share and is targeting a 20 percent share over the long term.

Analysts attribute the windfall to a DRAM supply shortage and price increases driven by AI server investment, and the companies are reinvesting it. YMTC reportedly has 4,796 R&D staff, has spent 14.2 billion yuan on R&D over three years, and holds 5,611 registered invention patents. It is using its Xtacking wafer bonding technology to work around U.S. export controls on advanced chipmaking equipment. The article notes that Samsung Electronics reportedly signed a related patent licensing agreement with YMTC last year. The report also says CXMT's July stock market listing raised a large sum that adds to its investment capacity.

The article cautions that a rising market share does not yet mean the technology gap is closing. CXMT's DDR5 products are reported to carry manufacturing costs per unit of data capacity more than 30 percent higher than those of Korean and U.S. producers. Analysts quoted in the report say the threat to Korean companies depends on when China's capacity additions take full effect, with some pointing to 2028 as the turning point. If large volumes of new Chinese output arrive as AI investment growth slows, the article says, commodity memory prices could come under downward pressure.

Articles.Title: AI Memory Boom Is Funding China's Chip Catch-Up - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Jay Y. Lee Visits UAE to Expand Samsung's Middle East AI Data Center Push
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee traveled to the United Arab Emirates, where he visited the construction site of the Al Dhafra gas-fired power plant in Abu Dhabi on November 21, local time, as the company reported on October 22. The trip was his first to the Middle East since he accompanied President Lee Jae-myung to the UAE last November. He toured major facilities at the plant, reviewed the construction schedule and safety management, and met with employees. At the site, he also held a meeting with executives from Samsung C&T and Samsung E&A on business strategy and new market entry.

Samsung said it is expanding its existing nuclear power and combined-cycle gas power businesses in line with the UAE's industrial development. The company is also looking for chances to join future projects in AI data centers and energy infrastructure. The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar are moving quickly to build data centers and power plants as AI adoption spreads across the region. Samsung Electronics, Samsung C&T and Samsung SDS plan to take part in designing, building and operating AI data centers. They also plan to supply advanced semiconductors and cooling equipment and to help construct power plants.

The company framed the visit as part of a push to move the group into new local businesses in a region the articles describe as still unsettled by war. Lee's presence at the site and his talks with the affiliate executives signal that the group is directing senior attention to the effort. The articles do not give investment amounts, contract values or timelines for any new AI data center or energy project. They also do not report any agreement signed during the visit. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Micron Q4 Cash Flow Hits $44B as vHBM Hype Builds [2026]
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology reported that it generated roughly $44 billion of operating cash flow in its fiscal fourth quarter, a figure its Chief Financial Officer, Mark Murphy, laid out on the fiscal Q4 earnings call. Against that, capital expenditures came to $10.8 billion, leaving free cash flow of $33.2 billion. The year-earlier quarter, which ended August 28, 2025, produced $5.73 billion of operating cash flow, so the new figure is nearly eight times higher. Micron had scheduled the report for September 30, 2026.

The comparison with fiscal 2025 is the clearest measure of the jump. Micron generated $17.53 billion of operating cash flow across all of fiscal 2025, which means the latest quarter alone exceeded that full-year total by roughly 2.5 times. The year-earlier free cash flow was labeled "adjusted" at $803 million, while the new figure is simply stated as free cash flow, so the two may not be defined identically. Murphy also reported customer cash deposits of $12.3 billion received during the quarter. Whether those deposits sit inside the operating cash flow total is not stated in the sources reviewed.

Murphy presented these figures as part of Micron's own financial results, and the numbers come from his remarks on the earnings call. Market coverage on platforms such as TradingView has also reported a wave of bullish analyst ratings, but the sources reviewed do not name the firms, the price targets, or the dates of those ratings. A separate write-up on X attributes a roadmap comment about vertical high-bandwidth memory appearing in 2028 to Sumit Sadana, Micron's Chief Business Officer. Micron's official results documents do not confirm that product name or date, so that claim remains secondhand.

Memory is a capital-intensive, cyclical business, and cash flow can swing sharply with prices, which is why the durability of this quarter's results is an open question. The sources do not say how Micron plans to deploy the cash, whether through capacity, debt reduction, or shareholder returns. Investors will be watching how much of the $12.3 billion in customer deposits converts into recognized revenue in later quarters. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Micron Q4 Cash Flow Hits $44B as vHBM Hype Builds [2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: ServiceNow’s Moment of Truth: Can Agentic AI Growth Justify a Premium 80x Earnings Multiple on Oct. 28?
stories.Summary:
ServiceNow is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, October 28, and the report has drawn attention because the stock trades at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 96 times. Shares rose about 12 percent over the past week as investors built expectations around the company's agentic AI business. The company has beaten earnings estimates for six straight quarters, most recently posting non-GAAP earnings of $0.90 per share against a consensus of $0.8564. Revenue rose 24.0 percent to $3.987 billion in that quarter, and management said its ServiceNow AI product crossed $1 billion in annual contract value.

The article notes that the last beat came with caveats, since management said about half of it came from U.S. Federal on-premise revenue pulled forward from the third quarter. It also flagged a roughly $35 million foreign exchange drag on third-quarter current remaining performance obligations. For the coming quarter, guidance calls for subscription revenue of $3,975 million to $3,980 million, current remaining performance obligations growth of 19.5 percent, and a 31 percent non-GAAP operating margin. The company is said to be on track to beat its $1.5 billion year-end AI contract value target. Bears argue that AI agents could reduce the number of paid seats, a concern the company answers by pointing to pricing.

Bill McDermott, the company's chief executive, reportedly said that about 50 percent of net new business is already non-seat-based and that AI-native products carry price premiums of 20 to 30 percent. The article quotes him as saying customers pay for resolutions rather than tokens, which is his way of framing the pricing model. The writer, Rich Duprey, presents the upcoming report as a test of whether clean AI and remaining performance obligations figures can justify the premium valuation. He also cites the 81 percent subscription gross margin guidance, which reflects hyperscaler and AI consumption costs.

The article places the report in the context of the stock's volatility, noting that shares fell about 17.75 percent on the day of the previous quarter's report after a slim beat. It describes the current valuation as already assuming that AI growth keeps compounding. The article does not say what the stock will do after the report, and it contains no price target. Investors will get the first concrete answer when the company reports its results on October 28.

Articles.Title: ServiceNow’s Moment of Truth: Can Agentic AI Growth Justify a Premium 80x Earnings Multiple on Oct. 28?

stories.Headline: Professor Kim Jung-ho: "South Korea's Chip Success Wasn't Just Technology—It Was a Windfall… HBM Was Decisive"
stories.Summary:
Professor Kim Jung-ho of Yonsei University has argued that South Korea's semiconductor success came from unexpected external factors as much as from technical skill. In a recent appearance on a YouTube channel, he said the flagship businesses of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix benefited from the AI boom in ways their original plans had not anticipated. He noted that Samsung aimed to lead in system semiconductors and saw its market share decline, while DRAM, its traditional mainstay, unexpectedly boomed as AI grew. He described the result as less a feat South Korea pulled off than a windfall that arrived on its own.

SK Hynix's investment in high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, was another example he gave. HBM stacks multiple DRAM chips vertically to raise data processing speed and efficiency, which makes it important for AI chips that need heavy computation. Kim said SK Hynix kept developing HBM even while the company was under financial strain. HBM initially gained little traction in the gaming PC market, but demand changed once ChatGPT drove rapid growth in AI, since data centers needed high-performance GPUs and memory that could keep pace with them. Kim summed up the value of HBM by saying it resolves the bottleneck in which GPUs run fast but memory cannot keep up.

Kim also pointed to possible openings for South Korea's battery industry. Chinese companies dominate electric vehicle batteries through mass production and price competitiveness, but he argued a different landscape could emerge in physical AI fields such as robotics. Because human-sized robots have limited room for batteries, high energy density matters, and he said South Korean batteries hold an advantage there. He also highlighted solid-state batteries, which address limits of conventional liquid-electrolyte designs, and said South Korea and Japan are strong contenders in commercializing them. He named defense combined with AI and drones as the next industry to develop, and stressed the need to reform education so that people can master AI.

Ahead of these discussions, the Smart Energy Plus (SEP) 2026 conference is scheduled for the 29th at COEX in Gangnam District, Seoul, where senior executives from both companies will speak about the future of AI and semiconductors. Han Jae-jun, a master, or managing director, at Samsung Electronics' AX/PI Center, will present a strategy for integrating AI from design through production, and Samsung will disclose a case in which automated techniques cut design time by about 50%. Choi Jun-yong, vice president of HBM business planning at SK Hynix, will discuss how the performance bottleneck has moved from computing to memory and now to power. He will address the "Energy Wall" created by rising data center power use and propose solutions such as higher bandwidth per watt and 3D stacking. Kim's analysis suggests that investment decisions should weigh how unpredictable AI demand is reshaping memory markets, not just the planned success of any one technology.

Articles.Title: Professor Kim Jung-ho: "South Korea's Chip Success Wasn't Just Technology—It Was a Windfall… HBM Was Decisive" - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: The Department of Health – Abu Dhabi publishes AI Clinician Framework to guide responsible research into AI clinician systems
stories.Summary:
The Department of Health – Abu Dhabi, the regulator of healthcare in the emirate, has published an AI Clinician Framework, which it describes as a world-first regulatory framework. The framework sets out how AI clinician systems may eventually be authorized to carry out clinical activities that currently require a licensed clinician. It was published in an article dated October 22, 2026, on globaltimes.cn. Under the framework, an AI clinician system is judged on its competence for the specific clinical activities it would perform. Systems seeking a wider clinical scope would need stronger evidence and demonstrated competence before being considered.

The framework requires safeguards at every level of clinical scope, including physician oversight and accountability and referral to a physician when needed. It also serves as the basis for future DoH policies and supporting standards. Those future policies and standards are expected to define which clinical activities an AI clinician system could be authorized to perform. They will also set out the evidence required at each stage and the thresholds against which such systems would be evaluated.

The articles do not name a specific official who spoke on the framework, so responsibility rests with the DoH as the publishing regulator. The framework is presented as a means of guiding responsible research into AI clinician systems. The articles provide no timetable for when the future policies or standards will be issued, and they do not say whether any AI clinician system has yet been submitted for authorization. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The Department of Health – Abu Dhabi publishes AI Clinician Framework to guide responsible research into AI clinician systems - Global Times

stories.Headline: AI products fuel spending during National Day holiday
stories.Summary:
During the weeklong National Day holiday in early October, shoppers across China crowded into stores to try the latest artificial intelligence gadgets, as smart devices continue moving from showrooms into the mass market. At Z. Pilot, an AI experience store in Shanghai, a furry AI pet robot drew a steady stream of browsers, with its digital eyes lighting up in a feeding expression when offered a toy carrot. Employees said companionship products were selling well, since the pets offer voice and touch interaction and gradually adapt to their owners over time. AI glasses, which handle real-time translation, navigation, teleprompting and photo and video capture, also drew strong interest in the city.

Demand reached beyond Shanghai. At a JD.com mall in the Qibao area, families gathered around 3D printers, and parents said they bought them so children could design and print their own models at home. In Hangzhou, a tech mall called Wensan brought together more than 700 smart products, from AI companion robots and AI glasses to smart rings and exoskeletons, for consumers of all ages. In Beijing, a robotics and AI experience brand under Shoucheng Holdings operates eight stores offering more than 200 robot and AI hardware products, and it drew long queues during the holiday, with particularly strong results for companion-style AI, entertainment devices and interactive robotics. Retailers are also reporting measurable gains: according to Suning.com, foot traffic at its flagship stores rose 50 percent year on year from October 1 to 7, while sales of AI-equipped home appliances climbed more than 40 percent, and smartwatches, AI glasses and action cameras all posted solid increases.

The article ties this consumer surge to a wider AI expansion in China. It reports that AI enterprises in the country passed 6,000 last year and that China had more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units, or 84.7 percent of the global market, according to an industry research report. Government policy has also pushed the trend forward: in June, eight departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, issued guidance to boost AI-enabled consumption, and a later action plan on smart home consumption let localities set their own subsidy categories and standards under the 2026 trade-in policy, including support for whole-house smart home purchases. Fan Chunyan, vice-president of Suning.com, said consumer uptake of AI products is moving from novelty toward mass adoption and that demand for smart devices, immersive experiences and ongoing services will keep rising.

Articles.Title: AI products fuel spending during National Day holiday - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Nasdaq & Chip Stocks Plunge: Jensen Huang’s Stock Touting Fails as Market Delivers Heavy Blow to AI Bulls
stories.Summary:
On October 22, Thursday, U.S. chip and tech stocks sold off sharply, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 2.6% in its largest single-day drop since June and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sliding about 6.72%. Shares of NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Micron and TSMC all slumped, and Meta's stock fell nearly 7%. The move followed Meta's quarterly report, in which heavier capital spending pushed its free cash flow negative to 2.12 billion U.S. dollars. Oil prices rose on Middle East tensions, adding to worries about inflation and interest rates.

The selloff did not come out of nowhere. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had already fallen for eight straight trading days through October 16, losing more than 15% in total. Data from Goldman Sachs' prime brokerage showed hedge funds cutting tech holdings at the fastest pace in at least ten years in the five sessions ending October 15, with semiconductors among the biggest reductions. Retail investors, by contrast, were buying chip, storage and AI cloud stocks on the dip, according to JPMorgan strategist Arun Jain's flow data for October 15 to 21.

Several prominent market figures voiced concern about the spending. Citadel founder Ken Griffin told foreign media on October 20 that investors are almost certain there is an AI bubble, comparing GPUs to airlines with very low marginal costs that could see prices fall if supply outpaces demand. He also noted that businesses are scrutinizing AI bills from firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI and want clear productivity gains, while still arguing that the leading companies will matter for decades. Michael Burry, who gained fame for betting against the housing market, has reportedly moved most of his short exposure into Nasdaq 100 and semiconductor ETF puts, and he believes a major market top could arrive within nine months.

Leverage amplified the pain. CoinGlass data cited by CoinDesk showed about 51.6 million U.S. dollars of chip-linked crypto perpetual contracts were liquidated within 10 minutes during the U.S. stock holiday on October 17, with about 38 million dollars from long positions. Short sellers of new AI cloud and data center companies, including CoreWeave and Nebius, have earned large paper profits this month, according to ORTEX, with roughly 6 billion dollars in total gains. Yet the broader market was not uniformly weak, since nearly two-thirds of S&P 500 stocks closed higher on October 22 even as the index fell 1.21%.

Articles.Title: Nasdaq & Chip Stocks Plunge: Jensen Huang’s Stock Touting Fails as Market Delivers Heavy Blow to AI Bulls - 36Kr

stories.Headline: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, working with collaborators at the University of Pennsylvania, developed LitPivot, a system that helps researchers revise early-stage research ideas as they read the literature. The article, published on October 23, 2026, describes what it calls a literature-initiated pivot, a change in research direction prompted by reading prior work. The team said it will be presented at UIST 2026 in Detroit. Its aim is to connect developing an idea with deciding which literature to measure that idea against.

LitPivot works by splitting a proposal into a problem, a proposed contribution, and an evaluation plan, and grouping retrieved papers around whichever part is being edited. A researcher selects papers, requests an assessment, and reviews a suggested rewrite alongside excerpts that support the critique. The article says researchers can accept, edit, or reject suggestions and can request new papers or refresh the literature ranking. In a lab study with 17 researchers, domain experts rated proposals developed with LitPivot as better grounded in the literature than those built with a text editor and an AI chat tool.

Participants also reported a stronger understanding of the literature and greater improvements in novelty and usefulness. The work was carried out by the researchers at the Allen Institute for AI and the University of Pennsylvania, and the article is written in the first person plural by the team. The authors state that the tool is intended for early-stage ideation and that the approach could possibly extend to longer writing tasks, such as drafting a paper's introduction. They also describe a small follow-up study in which five researchers used LitPivot on their own projects during 30-minute sessions, with some using it to vet new ideas and others to refine the framing of mature ideas.

The authors frame the results as suggesting that LitPivot can support both early exploration and the refinement of an existing research direction. The article places LitPivot within a broader set of tools from the same institute, including Theorizer, AutoDiscovery, HARPA, Scideator, and IdeaSynth, all part of the Asta effort. It also points to a separate study, Old Ideas, Novel Problems, which the authors say shows the limits of automated novelty evaluation. The article does not describe any further release timeline or plans beyond the conference presentation and the hope that the insights help scientists turn early ideas into new contributions.

Articles.Title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape

stories.Headline: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
stories.Summary:
Hugging Face published a post on October 23, 2026, announcing a lookup tool that shows whether popular Transformers models run on AWS Trainium. The tool is a Space called torch-neuronx model support, built by David Corvoysier and the Hugging Face team, which builds on the TorchNeuron backend introduced in an earlier post. Because Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium the way it does on other hardware, any model on the Hub may run there, but the Space records which ones have actually been tested. Its results come from a public dataset, aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support, which is updated with one Parquet file for each pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

The Space opens on a Selected view, a set of models chosen from the top Hub models by downloads and trending score, and each entry lists the result, the number of Trainium cores used, the wall time including compilation, and the peak device memory. Users can switch to Trending or Downloads views to search by name, and models left out are labeled with a reason, either low priority or true incompatibility. The Space also lets users choose which versions of the Neuron compiler and Transformers to examine. Each model page gives the tested Neuron stack, the packages to install, and a run.py script that loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when needed, and generates with a static cache and torch.compile using the neuron backend.

A cached set of compiled graphs can be downloaded from a public bucket to skip the first-run compilation. The authors state that testing covers only Transformers models, and only text-generation and image-text-to-text models in the current selection, with plans to add diffusers, sentence transformers, and other tasks. Each test runs on a trn2 instance across the fewest Trainium cores that can hold the weights, at most 16 cores, which means models must fit on four Trainium2 devices. The test generates 32 tokens, and on a single core they are compared with output from a CPU run of the same checkpoint, while sharded models are checked by a small judge model for fluent English.

The authors note that a pass says nothing about throughput or longer generations. Hugging Face says the Space will expand its coverage over time, and users can query the underlying dataset directly with pandas to check any model's result, neuronx_cc version, and core count. The dataset card explains the exact meaning of each result. Readers wanting the details can consult the Space and the dataset card for the current list of tested models.

Articles.Title: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

stories.Headline: Music Tectonics Returns Next Week With AI, Artist Revenue, and Our Future on the Agenda
stories.Summary:
The Music Tectonics conference returns to Santa Monica, California, from October 27 to 29, 2026, bringing together artists, entrepreneurs, investors, and music industry executives. Its theme is "Rising Tide: Growing Music, Growing Value," and organizers are asking how technology can help more people build a sustainable business in music. The three-day program covers artificial intelligence, direct-to-fan business models, royalty collection, investment, and new ways of connecting music with audiences. The event was announced in a Hypebot article published on October 23, 2026.

Artificial intelligence is a central focus of the program, with representatives from Stability AI, Suno, ElevenLabs, and Musical AI scheduled to discuss creativity, licensing, attribution, and business uses. On October 27, Roland's vice president of innovation, Paul McCabe, and Stability AI's chief executive, Prem Akkaraju, will take part in a fireside conversation about how technology companies and creators can build trust and develop AI responsibly. Merck Mercuriadis will give a keynote on October 28 that adds a view from music rights and monetization. Beyond AI, the sessions address practical concerns for independent artists, including reaching fans, collecting revenue, and financing a career.

Music Tectonics founder and director Dmitri Vietze says the organizers want to look at AI from several angles. Their aim is to bring creators, rights holders, and technology companies into the same conversations about the opportunities and challenges ahead. Vietze has also written an opinion piece for Hypebot titled "A Rising Tide Lifts All Boats." The article identifies him as the person responsible for shaping the conference's direction.

The program includes sessions such as "Direct to Fan in 2027," "Closing the Royalty Collection Gap," and "Don't Sell Before You Know Your Options," along with discussions of music on Roblox and where music technology investors are putting their money. An October 27 Creator Fair will feature creators including Hunna G, Modern Biology, and Chuck Sutton, focusing on the relationship between creative tools and human expression. Attendees can also meet potential collaborators and compare approaches with people building and using new music tools. Full program and registration details are available on the conference website.

stories.Headline: Tech Quiz Online | AI Inference Engineer
stories.Summary:
The articles do not describe a news event. They are a promotional page from TechGig, published on October 16, 2026, that advertises an online screening quiz called "Tech Quiz Online" for the role of AI Inference Engineer. The quiz assesses a candidate's ability to optimize, serve, and scale AI inference systems in production, and it is said to cover foundations, applied judgement, responsible AI, and job-ready evidence. Candidates start with screening and then receive a role scorecard and a path to the next round.

The page sets out what the role involves: designing and operating inference stacks for latency, throughput, and cost targets, applying quantisation, batching, caching, and routing, instrumenting production systems, and working with platform and model teams on rollout and capacity planning. Participants must register with a valid account before the published deadline, complete each round within its start and end window, and make only one active attempt per round unless extra attempts are granted. The quiz itself has 20 multiple-choice questions, with 60 seconds per question, 5 marks for each correct answer, no negative marking, and one attempt per question. Using unfair means results in disqualification, and organizers' decisions on scoring, ranking, and disqualification are final.

The page names TechGig as the platform and says the organizers may change the schedule, format, or prizes with prior notice. It also says rewards and opportunities are subject to eligibility checks and sponsor approval, that personal data is used only for program operations and communication, and that organizers are not liable for technical problems beyond their reasonable control. The page additionally offers a digital readiness badge after screening, weekly role-specific scenarios, invitations for top performers to a practical hackathon or system-design round, and community and referral features. It cites category-level AI hiring indicators from foundit Insights Tracker, Naukri JobSpeak, and the AWS GenAI Adoption Index, and states these are not role-specific hiring guarantees. The articles do not say how many people have registered, when the deadline falls, or what prizes are on offer.
