stories.Headline: Who Is Accountable When AI Makes the Decision?
stories.Summary:
This article is not a news report of an event. It is a promotional page for a free 60-minute online masterclass on AI accountability, published by TechGig on 23 October 2026. The session is scheduled for 23 November, from 11:00 AM to 12:00 PM, and is led by Dr. Smrite Goudhaman, described as a Global Professor of Practice at Golden Gate University and a Pre-Sales Solutions leader at Datamatics. It is aimed at people building or deploying AI, people signing off on AI releases, and people using AI in recruitment and screening. Participants who complete the session receive a Certificate of Participation.

The masterclass says it will help attendees explain who is accountable when an AI system makes or influences a consequential decision, such as rejecting a job candidate or affecting patient care. It promises to distinguish principles, voluntary guidance, national strategies and binding law across countries, including India, the European Union, the United States and the African Union. Attendees will work through a five-question Accountability Test on a hypothetical AI-assisted hiring decision, and the session covers where people can review, override, stop or appeal a decision. The organisers say no technical or legal background is needed, and that participants will leave with five questions to ask before deploying any AI system.

The articles do not report any incident, regulatory action or harm that prompted the session. The only named responsibility is Dr. Goudhaman's role as presenter, and the page states that it does not imply endorsement by the organisations it discusses. The page also cites her prior work, including a moderated side event at the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva and mentoring of learners towards UNESCO Ethics of AI coursework, but these are described as background rather than as findings. The articles do not say what happens after the session beyond the Q&A and the certificate.

Articles.Title: Who Is Accountable When AI Makes the Decision? - TechGig

stories.Headline: Harness launches AI Budgets to manage spending
stories.Summary:
Harness, a software company, introduced AI Budgets, a new feature within its Cost Management Agent, according to reports published on October 20 and October 23, 2026. The tool is designed to help organizations monitor and enforce limits on artificial intelligence spending. The company says that many organizations have AI cost policies but have no method to check whether those policies are followed. It cited its 2026 State of AI in FinOps Report, which found that 73 per cent of organizations have an AI cost policy while only 13 per cent can verify that it works.

AI Budgets lets organizations set spending limits by team, developer, model, or project, and it tracks spending as it occurs. Users receive a warning when spending reaches 90 per cent of a budget, which does not restrict access. Once spending exceeds 100 per cent of the weekly limit, access is paused until the next weekly reset or until an increase is approved. Smaller budget increase requests can be approved quickly within the product, while larger ones go to authorized approvers. The system records warnings, blocks, and approved increases in an immutable audit trail that can be exported for compliance programs including SOC 2 and ISO 27001.

Harness says it chose a weekly cycle instead of a monthly one because a monthly limit can let a team use most of its planned spending early in the month. The company tested the feature on its own AI tooling bill before opening early access. In that test, average weekly AI spending per developer fell from $184 to $115, a reduction of about 37 per cent. Cost per million tokens stayed near $1.80 through most of June and July, then dropped to $0.80 during the week governance was introduced, a decline of about 55 per cent. The product also tracks spending by user, provider, model, and token type, and it draws cost and usage data from multiple AI providers into one view.

The company says the feature is aimed at FinOps practitioners and engineering leaders. Harness states that FinOps teams can use it to enforce existing spending policies without manually reviewing every exception, while engineering leaders can use it to expand AI use within set limits. The policy engine is the same one used for cloud spending, and it connects to the Harness Software Delivery Agent, which can pause a deployment that would exceed a budget before the related spending occurs. AI Budgets is available now within the Cost Management Agent, and Harness says it is meant to move AI cost policies from written guidance to enforceable limits.

Articles.Title: Harness launches AI Budgets to manage spending - TechGig

stories.Headline: Indian entrepreneur unveils AI model for engineering design, claims cost advantage
stories.Summary:
Skyfall AI, a company co-founded by Indian entrepreneur Sam Pasupalak, has introduced SKY-001, an AI model built for complex engineering work using computer-aided design (CAD) and building information modelling (BIM). The article, published on October 22, 2026 by TechGig, reports that the model was unveiled by Pasupalak, who is the company's CEO. The model is the product of 18 months of work by the Skyfall AI team. Pasupalak says SKY-001 is faster, cheaper, and more accurate than the leading AI systems his team tested. SKY-001 is designed to produce complete product designs by working in stages, according to Skyfall AI.

For a complex product, the model first divides it into assemblies and individual components, then maps out how each part should be built using visual representations, sketches, and construction steps. For building design, it takes a building outline and breaks it into units and rooms. The company says this approach lets the model manage projects involving hundreds or thousands of steps while keeping each component consistent with the overall design. Pasupalak claims the model runs between 51 and 125 times faster than the frontier models tested. He also says it is more than 150 to 210 times cheaper, depending on the comparison.

Pasupalak's own cost comparison puts SKY-001 at $0.005 per sample for a CAD task, compared with $0.75 for GPT-6 Astra, a figure that makes GPT-6 Astra's cost 150 times higher. On accuracy, the company reports a score of 79.7 per cent on the Intersection over Union (IoU) metric, which measures how closely an AI-generated design overlaps a reference design, against 79.1 per cent for GPT-6 Astra. The article stresses that these figures come from Skyfall AI's own tests and have not been independently verified. It also notes that the results apply only to the engineering tasks tested and do not show that SKY-001 outperforms general-purpose AI models in other uses.

Pasupalak is originally from Bhubaneswar, Odisha, and is now based in San Francisco. Pasupalak started Skyfall AI in 2025, after co-founding the AI research startup Maluuba in 2011 and serving as its CEO. Microsoft acquired Maluuba in 2017, and at the company Pasupalak led researchers and engineers working on artificial intelligence and language understanding. The article does not say whether SKY-001 will be released publicly, what pricing it will carry, or when independent testing might be carried out.

Articles.Title: Indian entrepreneur unveils AI model for engineering design, claims cost advantage - TechGig

stories.Headline: Why smaller CPA firms may have the AI advantage
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, but an opinion column published on Accounting Today on October 23, 2026, by Adam Hale, a partner at Anders CPAs + Advisors and co-founder of Summit CPA Group. Hale argues that small CPA firms worried about falling behind larger firms in artificial intelligence are likely overestimating the gap, since AI accounting tools are advancing quickly in tax and audit software. He cites a Wolters Kluwer finding that 70% of all accounting firms already use AI at least weekly, a figure that rises only to 76% among high-growth firms. The column also notes that a three-year, $1 billion AI spending plan announced by PwC in 2023 does not automatically produce visible results.

Hale draws on a new Gartner CFO survey to show that uncertainty about AI returns is widespread across industries. In that survey, 55% of respondents reported positive overall returns on last year's AI investments, while 57% were unclear about which AI use cases produced those results. Hale says large, private equity-backed firms face their own obstacles, because their size spreads their deployments across many areas and makes return on investment harder to track. He argues that these conditions give smaller practices room to test processes and adjust quickly. The column does not present any new figures on the size of the advantage or any regulatory change.

Hale's central point is that small firms also face pressure from clients who now build their own AI-generated analyses and expect their accountants to review them. He says that CPAs find it hard to validate client-built tools that have not been properly designed, so smaller firms can gain an edge by creating their own reliable tools with proper expertise and safeguards. His advice is for firms to identify advisory gaps affecting their largest clients and to begin testing tools and workflows that supplement existing analysis. The column is written by an industry practitioner and offers his own view, and it does not report any planned events or next steps beyond that advice.

Articles.Title: Why smaller CPA firms may have the AI advantage - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: Micron: HBM’s Margin Drag Flips Into A Profit Driver In 2027 (NASDAQ:MU)
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology, Inc. (MU) is the subject of a Seeking Alpha analysis published on October 23, 2026, by analyst Rick Orford, who retains a Strong Buy rating on the stock. The article follows a blowout quarter that Micron reported after Orford's previous piece on September 18, when the stock traded at $977.50. Orford states that the company's guidance calls for 22% sequential weekly revenue growth and that margins are expected to bottom in fiscal 2027 before improving. He also cites a valuation of 5.6 times earnings as part of the case for the stock. The article points to a $35.16 billion buyback authorization that becomes available on December 9, 2026, which Orford says is sized off real cash and is well covered by Micron's balance sheet.

The margin pressure the headline describes comes from high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, which the author expects to turn into a profit driver as HBM pricing rises. Orford presents the margin dip as temporary, with the bottom coming in fiscal 2027 and improvement following. The buyback and the margin recovery together form the core of the bullish argument in the piece. Orford acknowledges risks, including competition from China's CXMT, which he says is targeting high-margin DRAM. He writes that current price levels already discount much of the potential downside from that competition.

The analysis is written in his own first-person opinion, and he states that he holds no position in Micron and receives no compensation beyond Seeking Alpha's payments. Seeking Alpha's own disclaimer notes that the views expressed may not reflect the platform's position and that past performance is no guarantee of future results. The article does not describe any specific next event beyond the December 9, 2026 date when the buyback authorization unlocks. Its forward-looking claims about margins and HBM pricing are presented as expectations rather than confirmed outcomes. Readers would need to watch Micron's subsequent quarterly results to see whether the projected fiscal 2027 margin bottom and recovery materialize.

Articles.Title: Micron: HBM’s Margin Drag Flips Into A Profit Driver In 2027 (NASDAQ:MU) - Seeking Alpha

stories.Headline: ASML's Hybrid Bonding Patents Reveal a Carousel Design Aimed at BESI's Turf
stories.Summary:
ASML has filed patents for a hybrid bonding tool that reverses the usual setup, according to SemiAnalysis analysts Howie and Sherry Zhang, who examined the filings. Instead of a robotic head picking up each die and placing it on a stationary wafer, the wafer rises to meet dies riding a conveyor track. The design borrows more from front-end lithography than from today's pick-and-place bonders, which could put ASML in direct competition with BESI. Hybrid bonding is becoming central to performance gains as transistor scaling slows, so the choice of tool stack matters to major logic customers.

In conventional die-to-wafer tools from BESI or ASMPT, the base wafer stays still while a bond head lifts, aligns and presses each die into place. ASML's design moves the dies on a carrier past measurement and plasma activation stations, with a chuck lifting the wafer to meet each die at the bonding station. The analysts say the track hardware comes from SuperTrak Conveyance, a startup they researched. Sherry Zhang said the timing is several years away but still worth discussing because the architecture differs sharply from current tools. Howie described ASML's overlay precision as far higher than pick-and-place systems, though the moving-track approach raises open questions about measurement accuracy and cleanliness across a track spanning several meters.

The analysts also restated their February 2024 view that HBM will not adopt die-to-wafer hybrid bonding before 2029, if at all, because the economics fail against thermo-compression bonding. For logic, they point to a Huawei phone chip, the 9050, as an early production example that runs up to 2.7 GHz without raising voltage or power. They are skeptical of vendor roadmaps, noting that ASML's earlier transistor-density projections never materialized and saying that claims about hybrid bonding in NAND and DRAM should be taken with a grain of salt. BESI's shares reportedly fell nearly 3% in Amsterdam when the research was published, while ASML rose.

Separately, the analysts describe how Huawei is pursuing full logic folding for data center accelerators by 2030, and how Chinese toolmakers including NAURA and AMEC are building hybrid bonding capability. Export controls could accelerate that localization, Sherry Zhang said, though she declined to predict policy. A related shift toward a 6x12 photomask, targeted for 2030, would restore full-reticle High-NA exposure and could feed into ASML's tool pricing, which management has said is value-based. Bits & Chips reports that BESI's hybrid-bonding orders in the first nine months of 2026 exceeded twice the total for all of 2025, with 23 customers and cumulative demand above 215 systems. CEO Richard Blickman said memory makers' interest is growing even as they delayed hybrid bonding in HBM.

Articles.Title: ASML's Hybrid Bonding Patents Reveal a Carousel Design Aimed at BESI's Turf - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Korea to Fast-Track AI Data Center Permits, Allow Driverless Car Sales
stories.Summary:
South Korea's government announced plans on October 23, 2026, to speed up permits for artificial intelligence data centers and loosen rules on self-driving vehicles. The changes were unveiled by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport at the second plenary meeting of the Regulatory Rationalization Committee, which the president chairs. The plans were reported by the Seoul Economic Daily. The science ministry will create a one-stop fast-track window for AI data center permits, which it describes as the biggest obstacle to building such facilities. Facilities outside the capital area that meet certain criteria would be exempted from power grid impact assessments.

Because areas where people are present make up less than 30% of an AI data center, unmanned spaces such as server rooms and cooling and power equipment would be excluded from building size calculations. The government also plans to spend 200 billion won next year on upstream and downstream industries and to designate AI data center special zones. Deputy Prime Minister Bae Kyung-hoon, who also heads the science ministry, told a parliamentary audit the same day that leased AI data centers currently receive no tax benefits and that the government would move quickly to discuss this with fiscal authorities. The transport ministry will create a legal framework for robotaxi operators and plans to finish revising the law by next year. Pilot robotaxi operations are expected to begin around 2028 in Gwangju, a test city for self-driving technology.

Sales channels for driverless cars are set to open starting at the end of this year, under new safety standards. Corporate testing rules will also be relaxed, allowing self-driving cars without a driver's seat to travel outside designated pilot zones when heading to a depot or recharging. Raw data collected by business vehicles operated by third parties will be made available for use. The article does not say how these measures will be enforced beyond the timelines listed. More details on the tax changes and the special zones are expected as the ministries finalize their plans.

Articles.Title: Korea to Fast-Track AI Data Center Permits, Allow Driverless Car Sales - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Kakao Mobility Unveils AI Parking Tech That Cuts Exit Times 20%
stories.Summary:
Kakao Mobility, a South Korean company, presented its artificial intelligence and data-driven parking technology at the 2026 ITS World Congress in Gangneung, where it served as an official sponsor. The company spoke on the 23rd of October, 2026, about its showing at the event, which was the world's largest gathering devoted to transportation technology and was held in South Korea for the first time in 16 years. Its exclusively sponsored session, held on the 22nd under the theme "Redefining Urban Parking," focused on connecting parking facilities into smart city infrastructure. The session was chaired by Park Dong-ju, president of the Korean Society of Intelligent Transport Systems.

Park Eun-ho, head of the Platform & Commerce business division, described how the company has linked parking facilities nationwide into one platform since launching its service in 2017. He highlighted barrier-free exits, which let drivers leave without stopping because payment is automatic, and the country's first cloud-based parking control system. Seo Jung-hoon, a director on the DeepAI team, presented AI that uses cameras to read license plates and parking spaces, along with 3D indoor and outdoor mapping and digital twin technology. The company also recently signed a proof-of-concept contract for Saudi Arabia's Diriyah smart city project, which marks a push into overseas markets.

Kim Gun-woo, head of the Future Platform Economy Research Institute, closed the session with an analysis of about 1.62 million parking-related data records. According to that analysis, platform-based tools such as the Kakao T parking pass and automatic payment eased bottlenecks when vehicles leave, cutting the interval between departing cars by up to about 20 percent. Hwang Yoon-young, head of compliance management at Kakao Mobility, said the congress gave the company a chance to share its AI, data and research with transportation officials from around the world. She also said the company will keep developing its parking technology as infrastructure for urban transport and for autonomous driving, and will expand further into global markets.

Articles.Title: Kakao Mobility Unveils AI Parking Tech That Cuts Exit Times 20% - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: From Argentina to Israel's AI research community: The journey of Claudia Goldman
stories.Summary:
Claudia V. Goldman, a computer scientist, has been an associate professor in the Data Science Department at the Hebrew University Business School in Jerusalem since July 2024, according to a Jerusalem Post profile published on October 24, 2026. Born in Buenos Aires, she made aliyah with her family in January 1984, when she was 16. She graduated from Mae Boyer High School in Jerusalem in 1986, did her army service, and then earned three degrees from the Hebrew University, including a PhD in Computer Science in 1999. Between 1999 and 2005 she held research posts at Bar-Ilan University, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, and the University of Haifa. She then moved into industry, working three years as a team leader at Samsung Telecom Research in Herzliya and 15 years as a research scientist at General Motors' research and development organization in Herzliya.

The article credits her with 24 patents and more than 50 academic papers. Her work at General Motors included introducing learning agents into the vehicle user experience so drivers could stay focused on the road. In her classroom, Goldman sets clear rules on when students may use AI tools and requires them to credit the tools and explain how they were used. She asks students not to submit answers generated entirely by AI, and to test AI responses for bias and for whether cited sources actually exist. Her grading combines in-class work, presentations, and student-run discussions so she can assess understanding directly.

Asked about a idea from Bill Gates of reserving some jobs for humans, she said the question is not a simple split between human and AI professions but one of understanding where AI helps in different contexts. The interview is framed as a profile rather than a news event, and the article does not describe any upcoming changes or policy decisions. It notes that Hebrew University offers a Free Listener Program that lets senior citizens audit courses, with the fall semester just beginning. The piece also recounts her family history, including grandparents who came to Argentina before relatives were murdered in the Holocaust, and her marriage in 1999 to Prof. Roy Shenhar, a chemistry professor at the same university.

Articles.Title: From Argentina to Israel's AI research community: The journey of Claudia Goldman

stories.Headline: Big Tech Can't Stop AI Spending, but the Cash Is Running Out
stories.Summary:
Big Tech's push into artificial intelligence is running into a financing squeeze, according to a Seoul Economic Daily report published on October 23, 2026. The reporters, Kim Chang-young and Cho Yang-joon, say the largest technology companies have used up internal cash, corporate bond sales and circular financing arrangements as their spending has ballooned. Even so, the companies maintain that demand for AI is overwhelming and that they cannot stop raising money. A Reuters report cited in the article projects that combined capital spending at Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle will reach $945.55 billion in January next year, roughly six times the January 2023 level. Over the same period, their free cash flow is expected to swing to a deficit of $2.87 billion from $223.11 billion.

Meta is at the center of the concern after disclosing commitments of nearly $825 billion to AI infrastructure. That figure includes $355.7 billion in operating and finance leases that do not appear on its balance sheet, along with $454.5 billion in separate non-cancelable contracts, including third-party cloud services. The total is $125 billion more than the $700 billion Meta disclosed at the end of July. Following the announcement, the premium on credit default swaps, which measures the risk of default, rose 8.9 basis points to 119.3 basis points. To raise funds quickly, Meta plans to issue non-voting Class C shares in January, first distributing one new share for each share held and later selling additional shares into the market.

Anthropic and OpenAI are also moving ahead with plans to go public despite heavy spending. Reuters reported that Anthropic may file its registration statement as early as the end of this month and hold its IPO in the middle of next month, after spending $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of this year alone. Its contractual obligations for computing power over the next decade total $450 billion, and that figure could reach $750 billion with ongoing negotiations. OpenAI, preparing an IPO next year, has reportedly lowered its valuation target to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion after some investors called the earlier figure too high. Meta has argued that large AI fundraising by Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI makes the market harder, so it needs to secure capital before rivals.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has said at a Berlin event that the constraint on AI expansion is financing rather than weak demand. He defended neocloud companies such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, which sit at the center of investor worries. Industry observers read Big Tech's moves as an attempt to draw more private capital through investment banks while counting on U.S. government support. The Trump administration issued an executive order in July last year offering loan guarantees, lending, subsidies, tax benefits and long-term purchase contracts for data centers, and the industry wants that support expanded. Analysts say aggressive use of these programs could ease the companies' funding strains.

Articles.Title: Big Tech Can't Stop AI Spending, but the Cash Is Running Out - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: From slop to non-slop: The new big AI theme is quantity
stories.Summary:
Two years ago, debate about AI centered on quality, with critics pointing to invented court cases, biased outputs, and images with six fingers. Those complaints have faded, though some still circulate, as when a single caught error is treated as a verdict on the whole technology. The article argues that such catches assume everyone can call on a top expert, which most people cannot. Meanwhile, a recent Microsoft result showed a panel of AI agents diagnosing hard medical cases correctly more than twice as often as generalist doctors working alone. The article's point is that such help can reach anyone, anywhere, at low cost.

The article describes a different kind of change, driven by sheer quantity rather than individual quality. In September, one lab ran roughly ten thousand agents on a famous open problem about the behavior of fluid flow equations, producing a proof in under four days. In October the same lab posted 722 manuscripts covering results in 372 families across mathematics, each costing on average a few hours of machine thinking. Other examples cited include a seventeenfold cut in quantum circuit operations, an eleven-day rewrite of a large programming tool into a new language, and about two thousand agents working through an eight-million-cell mouse brain atlas in thirty-two minutes. The author expects these volumes to keep rising as models get cheaper and more capable.

The article's central claim is that human attention and time used to pace every wave of invention, and that ceiling is now lifting. It warns that many results will emerge inside companies that never publish, and some may reach products before anyone can explain them. It also argues that quantity changes the arithmetic of failure, since a method that succeeds once in a thousand tries is likely to succeed at least once in three thousand when success can be recognized. The author says the greatest risk belongs to those who decide not to build the capacity to absorb this output.

The article presents these developments as an overall flood of useful output rather than a matter of mood or opinion. It notes that the examples so far come from a few weeks in late 2026, and that the models behind them are the weakest the world will use from here on. The author predicts that next year's systems will be cheaper, will hold more, and will run in larger numbers. The article ends by suggesting that the broader question is no longer whether machine output is flawless but how much of it society can use and check.

Articles.Title: From slop to non-slop: The new big AI theme is quantity

stories.Headline: Texas Athletics and McCombs School of Business Launch New Bevo Lab, Bringing Together Sports, AI and Analytics
stories.Summary:
Texas Athletics and the Business of Sports Institute at the McCombs School of Business announced the launch of Bevo Lab, a collaboration that will serve as a sports intelligence platform and living laboratory for the university. The announcement was made on October 23, 2026, in cooperation with Longhorn Sports Properties, and Vice President and Folger Family Athletics Director Chris Del Conte is set to formally unveil the lab at Texas' Business of College Sports Summit that day. The lab is meant to combine sports, technology, data analytics and artificial intelligence to improve human performance while giving students hands-on learning. It will draw on the university's 21 intercollegiate teams and more than 500 student-athletes.

The lab will house four main components: the Bevo Lakehouse, a unified data warehouse that will first consolidate football data such as game film and wearable technology before expanding to all 21 varsity sports. Predictive AI and analytics models will provide coaches with insights for game strategy, scouting and player development, including a "transfer AI" tool for roster evaluation. Tailored applications will give athletes, coaches and athletic executives interfaces built for their daily workflows. A skills-training program will let UT students build AI skills and deploy live applications alongside athletic teams, including through a Google Public Sector ambassador program. The lab will be housed in Innovation Tower near campus, and as many as 40 student researchers each year will work on its modeling and data projects.

Three companies have joined as sponsors. Dell Technologies is the founding sponsor and Official Technology Infrastructure Sponsor, supplying the secure AI-ready infrastructure, while Google Cloud is the Official Cloud Provider and Enterprise AI Provider, using its platform and Gemini models. SHI International serves as the strategic technology and solutions integrator, tying the partners' technologies into one platform. Del Conte called the effort a way to make Texas Athletics the most data-driven athletic program in the country, and Kirk Goldsberry, executive director of the institute, said the partners' tools would speed up data analysis. Google Cloud's Matt Renner, a UT alumnus, said the lab would set a new benchmark for sports innovation.

The announcement comes with early results and a stated plan for growth. The articles say early work with Google Public Sector has already introduced AI workflows that save UT coaches more than 15 hours per week in game preparation. Longhorn Sports Properties, the Austin-based division of Learfield, helped develop the lab and secured its corporate sponsors. More information is to be posted on a dedicated microsite at texaslonghorns.com/bevolab.

Articles.Title: Texas Athletics and McCombs School of Business Launch New Bevo Lab, Bringing Together Sports, AI and Analytics

stories.Headline: As the AI Buildout Slows Down, Here’s What to Do Next
stories.Summary:
Fauquier County in Virginia, west of the Washington, D.C. area known as Data Center Alley, has become a hard place to build AI data centers. Developers submitted nine business-park data center proposals there, but only one won approval. On October 8, the county's Board of Supervisors adopted new zoning rules that make data center construction more restrictive. The rules point to a growing set of obstacles for an industry that depends on borrowed money and tight timelines.

Developers face three kinds of obstacles, and each adds cost. Some localities have led projects to be canceled before construction started, including a 2.2-million-square-foot campus near Remington that was withdrawn. Amazon's $550 million data center in Warrenton, approved in February 2023, has been tied up in a lawsuit from residents for more than three years. The Remington Technology Park, approved in 2018, still cannot get enough power from the local grid, so the county approved a plan in July for natural gas fuel cells and backup diesel generators. Without that workaround, the project could be delayed until at least 2030.

The article frames these obstacles as a cost squeeze it calls the Expense Jaw, which rises with every court date, permit hurdle, and on-site power system. The author describes the risk in the same terms, noting that each delay pushes back the point at which a project begins to earn revenue. The article also notes that more than 300 towns, cities, and counties have adopted data center moratoriums or bans, according to the research firm SemiAnalysis. Gallup found that 7 in 10 Americans oppose a data center in their area, with electricity bills a major concern.

The article warns that the pressure could also come from the revenue side, which it calls the Revenue Jaw. As AI becomes cheaper to provide, competition could push down prices even as construction costs rise and debt payments come due. The author also cites the late investor Charlie Munger, who said that liabilities are always real while assets carry uncertainty. The article's broader point is that the buildout is continuing, but its timing and costs are becoming harder to predict. It says the demand for AI is real, and so are the obstacles to supplying it.

Articles.Title: As the AI Buildout Slows Down, Here’s What to Do Next

stories.Headline: DrizzVision’s AI App Testing Ambition Meets Reality
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru-based DrizzVision, a startup building AI for mobile app testing, has drawn attention for an ambitious product that still faces reliability questions. Its AI agent, Fathom, uses visual models to read app screens and carry out tests from plain-language instructions, rather than depending only on predefined element identifiers. The company's own benchmark shows performance falling sharply across different testing conditions. The story, published by Analytics India Magazine on October 24, 2026, examines how well that approach holds up in practice.

The company's roots lie in a familiar frustration with software development. Co-founder Yash said that teams often build quickly and then spend two to three days on end-to-end testing. Conventional tools such as Appium locate buttons through internal identifiers, so a renamed button or a redesigned screen can break a test even when the app still works. DrizzVision argues that its system instead interprets what is visible on screen, and it says it has cut test flakiness on an internal benchmark from between 15% and 50% to around 3%, while cautioning that results vary by client and use case. Yash also described how the system should handle pop-ups and changed icons without failing the test.

DrizzVision tested Fathom on Android across six model configurations and 20 tasks, running each task-model combination five times. In the easier suite, the models passed 217 of 300 scored runs, a 72.3% pass rate. On a harder suite using a rooted Android image, which let the grader inspect the app's database, they passed 86 of 300 runs, or 28.7%. The company said the image used for the first suite has since been retired, so it cannot rerun that test, and it noted that five of the ten harder tasks scored zero across every configuration without a full task-by-task explanation. DrizzVision cautions that these figures measure the whole system, including the model, its agent design and the Android image, rather than the model alone.

The article also covers data security, with Yash saying that screenshots should never leave the device, and noting that DrizzVision deploys its own models on-premise for clients. The company piloted an early command-line tool with Walmart, and its product is now offered through desktop, web, CI/CD pipelines and a command-line interface for AI coding assistants. Yash expects it to complement the open-source tool Maestro more often than replace it, and he suggests that verifying AI agents could become a larger future market. DrizzVision has raised $2.7 million in seed funding, has around 15 employees and says it has more than 10 enterprise customers, while the article notes that the agent verification service it describes does not yet exist as a product.

Articles.Title: DrizzVision’s AI App Testing Ambition Meets Reality - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Exclusive: Longhorns used AI against Florida — a 'new wave' for UT sports
stories.Summary:
The University of Texas Athletics Department is launching Bevo Lab, a sports intelligence platform that uses artificial intelligence across the department, with the official announcement set for Friday, October 23, 2026. The platform was first used during the fourth quarter of the Longhorns' game against Florida at Royal-Memorial Stadium last week, when Texas trailed 20-17 on a fourth-and-2. Coach Steve Sarkisian and his staff turned to Bevo Lab for help, but the Longhorns failed to convert after quarterback Arch Manning lost three yards on the play. The rollout begins with the football team, where the AI can offer coaches insight on game strategy, scouting, player development and recovery. Unlike general chatbots, the system uses only UT data.

Bevo Lab will store sports-specific information in a unified data center called the Bevo Lakehouse, which can include game film and readings from wearable devices such as heart rate monitors. Each team gets its own custom AI framework, so coaches like Sarkisian and women's basketball coach Vic Schaefer cannot access each other's data. The platform is expected to expand across all 21 varsity sports, and Athletic Director Chris Del Conte said it will bring together nutrition, sports science and mental health staff. Deputy Athletics Director Drew Martin said the platform is already helping coaches save time. The lab can support as many as 40 students each year, and its inaugural team includes 24 students selected through a hackathon.

Athletic Director Chris Del Conte called the initiative "the new wave" and said it would change college athletics, while Martin predicted it would fundamentally alter how programs use data. The lab is headquartered in UT's Innovation Tower and will be directed by Kirk Goldsberry, a former Spurs analytics executive who co-founded the Business Sports Institute. Dell Technologies, Google and SHI International are the founding partners, with Dell providing computing power, Google supplying its Cloud Platform and Gemini AI system, and SHI integrating the technology. Goldsberry said the goal is to give coaches good data so they can make informed decisions and win more competitions. The articles do not say how the Florida fourth-down play was ultimately evaluated, and they describe Bevo Lab's results so far only in general terms.

Articles.Title: Exclusive: Longhorns used AI against Florida — a 'new wave' for UT sports

stories.Headline: Few Americans Say They Are Asking AI Chatbots for 2026 Election Information
stories.Summary:
About one in ten U.S. adults, or 8%, say they are using AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini to find information about the 2026 elections. That finding comes from a Pew Research Center survey of 5,273 adults conducted from Oct. 12 to 18, 2026. The survey is part of the Center's American Trends Panel and is meant to show how Americans are turning to chatbots ahead of the midterms. Overall, about half of U.S. adults now use chatbots for various tasks, so the election use is a much smaller slice of that activity.

Among those who do use chatbots for election information, searching for facts is the most common purpose. Most of them say they use the tools to learn where candidates stand on the issues, which 76% reported. Roughly seven in ten, or 71%, say they use chatbots to check the accuracy of things they have read or heard elsewhere about candidates or issues. Around two-thirds, 65%, use them to learn about candidates' lives and careers.

Smaller shares ask for suggestions on how to vote, at 40%, or for help with registration, polling places or voting by mail, also at 40%. Use of chatbots for election information tracks closely with overall chatbot use across demographic groups. Adults under 50 are more likely than those 50 and older to use chatbots in general, and the same gap appears for election questions. Eleven percent of adults under 50 use chatbots for election information, compared with 4% of those 50 and older.

The survey shows these patterns as descriptive findings and does not go further into why the differences exist. The report was written by Ted Van Green, a research analyst focusing on U.S. politics and policy at Pew Research Center. Pew describes itself as a nonpartisan, nonadvocacy fact tank that does not take policy positions. The article provides the survey questions, detailed responses and methodology for readers who want to examine the data further.

Articles.Title: Few Americans Say They Are Asking AI Chatbots for 2026 Election Information

stories.Headline: American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce to 'prepare for AI'
stories.Summary:
American Express said on its third-quarter earnings call that it is cutting about 5% of its global workforce, a reduction of thousands of employees as the card company prepares for artificial intelligence to take over more internal processes. The announcement came from chairman and CEO Stephen Squeri on a Friday analyst call, with the firm taking a $336 million restructuring charge. Amex had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025. The cuts were reported by CNBC on October 23, 2026.

Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC that the restructuring was meant to make the company leaner and more agile and to prepare it for AI. He explained that the firm wants to reduce layers of management and widen spans of control before automating, since processes should be well structured before they are automated. The aim, he said, is to take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and years. Squeri said the charge was intended to improve efficiency and help the company accelerate innovation over the next few years.

Squeri spent part of his prepared remarks on AI, focusing mainly on using it to personalize experiences and offers for cardholders. He said Amex would meet customers' desire to use AI, including AI agents, but would not let assistants run unchecked through its systems. He said the company would allow agents to connect only through approved API or MCP channels, which are two ways of securely linking outside platforms to Amex systems. Le Caillec also said part of the restructuring was funded by proceeds from the sale of Amex's stake in Global Business Travel Group.

The company posted quarterly results that beat Wall Street profit expectations, with adjusted earnings of $4.68 per share against an analyst average of $4.48, according to LSEG. It raised its full-year earnings guidance to $18.30 to $18.60 per share on an unadjusted basis, up from $17.30 to $17.90. Total revenue rose 9% to $20.06 billion, slightly below the $20.12 billion LSEG forecast, and executives blamed part of the spending drag on recent exits from small business co-brand partnerships. The cuts follow a similar move by Barclays, which confirmed plans on the Thursday before to trim 5,000 jobs, also roughly 5% of its staff. Amex shares fell roughly 4% in afternoon trading.

Articles.Title: American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce to 'prepare for AI'

stories.Headline: Texas introduces Bevo Lab: AI-powered game-planning tool also evaluates portal targets, rev-share budgets
stories.Summary:
Texas announced on Friday, October 23, 2026, the creation of the Bevo Lab, a sports analytics and artificial intelligence hub on campus inside Austin's Innovation Tower. The 25,000-square-foot space is backed by Google Cloud, Dell Technologies and SHI International as founding corporate partners. Texas coaches already use a Google Gemini chatbot to answer questions about opponent tendencies, such as how often a team blitzes on third-and-5 or shorter. The university says early work with Google Public Sector has saved its coaches more than 15 hours a week in game preparation this season.

The lab will bring in up to 40 student researchers in its first year, growing to 200 a year, and 24 undergraduates have been hired for its first team, who begin training with Google next week. Athletic director Chris Del Conte said construction should finish in about three months, and Kirk Goldsberry, executive director of the Business of Sports Institute, said the lab will be fully operational in 2027. The system also covers the basketball transfer portal, where a tool grades players and projects how they would perform at Texas against an SEC schedule. Texas uses the data to help set revenue-sharing budgets, with Goldsberry saying the challenge is finding the best player within budget. The lab plans to pull in movement and wear-and-tear data from tracking companies, starting with football.

Goldsberry, who previously charted shots for ESPN's Grantland and worked for the San Antonio Spurs, said the Texas approach streamlined reports that staff once had to finish over weekends. Del Conte argued that data could challenge long-held play-calling habits, saying a coach's favorite play might turn out to be one of the least productive in certain situations. Goldsberry said the lab has built models rating roughly 5,000 men's and 5,000 women's college basketball players, which coaches Sean Miller and Vic Schaefer use. Matt Renner, president and chief revenue officer of Google Cloud and a Texas graduate, said other schools are not working with Google at this level. Del Conte said he hopes the model spreads to other schools.

Articles.Title: Texas introduces Bevo Lab: AI-powered game-planning tool also evaluates portal targets, rev-share budgets

stories.Headline: Jack Dorsey's new voice AI is impressing users and alarming fraud watchers
stories.Summary:
On October 24, 2026, CoinDesk reported that Block, the payments company led by Jack Dorsey, had unveiled a voice AI model called Dessa. According to Block's announcement, Dessa was trained entirely on human speech rather than text, and it can listen while it speaks, so it can handle interruptions, laughter and shifts in tone. Block says it trained the model from scratch on a single Nvidia GB200 NVL72 computing system, and the model is compact enough to run locally on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Max chip or better. Dessa is currently a research preview rather than a public product.

Company demonstrations, which Block says were recorded live without anyone steering the model's replies, drew strong reactions online. Dorsey wrote on X that talking with Dessa feels like talking with a person, full of emotion, nuance and natural pauses. Some users praised how human it sounded, and Binance founder Changpeng Zhao suggested it could help teach children through conversation in his GiggleAcademy project. Others warned that the same realism could be used to deceive people, with filmmaker Justine Bateman arguing it could help trick people into lowering their guard and journalist Shiv Aroor warning that scam calls could reach pandemic levels.

Block has not disclosed the model's size, benchmark results or a public release date, and the audio samples are company demonstrations rather than independent tests. The company is giving early access to a small group of AI safety researchers. Block argues that speech-based AI could eventually better recognize emotional cues such as distress and pain that text transcripts miss, while it assesses risks it may have overlooked. Dessa comes from Block's AI research lab, which reports directly to Dorsey and includes former staff from Dessa, the Toronto startup Square acquired in 2020.

Articles.Title: Jack Dorsey's new voice AI is impressing users and alarming fraud watchers

stories.Headline: US Air Force wants AI to assist aerial refueling
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Air Force is looking to artificial intelligence to help its aerial refueling crews improve their performance. The service wants AI to automatically analyze refueling operations recorded by cameras mounted on tankers and then give the tanker crews "hot wash" feedback. The plan appears in an Air Force Small Business Innovation Research solicitation, which the article describes as the vehicle for finding a system to do this work. The article, published October 23, 2026, is written by Michael Peck.

The solicitation asks for a system that uses computer vision, machine learning and flight dynamics analysis to pull performance measures from refueling events and flag deviations from the intended flight profile. The system would also produce post-flight feedback meant to sharpen aircrew skills, reduce mishaps linked to human factors and improve mission readiness. It would track the tanker, the refueling boom and the receiving aircraft, and measure position, velocity, alignment and closure rate. The article says the system would display results through AI overlays, heat maps, event timelines and interactive debriefs, and could link to virtual reality, simulators and other training tools. The Air Force describes the effort as a prototype for future AI-enabled training across the Department of Defense.

The solicitation is tied to the KC-46 tanker, which has a remote vision system that lets operators control the refueling boom through cameras and a 3D display. The article notes that this system has had teething problems, but the Air Force says most of them will soon be resolved. The service's stated reason for the change is that current training and post-flight reviews depend heavily on instructor observation, pilot self-assessment, manual video review and subjective judgment. The Air Force hopes an AI-based assessment will reduce the biases in those human evaluations of aerial refueling, which the article calls one of the most demanding tasks for aircrew.

The solicitation's stated end goal is an operationally demonstrated capability that is ready to implement for at least one type of receiver aircraft. It should also fit into existing aviation training systems and serve as a scalable base for AI-enabled performance assessment across the Department of Defense. The article does not say when the work would be awarded or fielded, and it does not name a contractor. What it does establish is that the Air Force is seeking a prototype first, with the aim of extending the approach to other aircraft and training programs if the prototype succeeds.

Articles.Title: US Air Force wants AI to assist aerial refueling

stories.Headline: How AI technology is giving ALS patients their voice back
stories.Summary:
Paul Francoeur, a 67-year-old Vermonter who was diagnosed with ALS in 2019, has regained a synthesized version of his own voice through AI voice-cloning technology from the company ElevenLabs. The story, published by InvestigateTV on October 23, 2026, describes how his wife Kris and son Ben helped him communicate as his illness weakened his muscles and speech. Before the new technology, he relied on eye-gaze software that spelled out words and produced a flat, robotic voice. Because the cloning process needed clear recordings from before his speech was affected, the family turned to a 2012 WCAX "Made in Vermont" segment about his spinning-wheel work. ElevenLabs said it needed only 16 seconds of audio from that story to recreate his voice.

The technology replaces the robotic output with a voice that sounds like Francoeur and can convey emotion. Richard Cave of ElevenLabs said the company is using AI to help people recreate their natural voices, and the company offers the service to ALS patients for free. The organization Bridging Voices helps families get connected with the company. The article notes that ALS has no cure and is always fatal, and that Vermont has the highest per capita rate in the country, with about 27 people living with the disease in the state.

Dr. Mark Garrett, who runs the ALS clinic at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and is Francoeur's doctor, said speech loss has a profound effect on quality of life. He praised the couple for their advocacy and suggested Francoeur's approach to his diagnosis may have contributed to surviving eight years, well beyond the typical two to five. Francoeur's first messages through the new voice were a thank-you and an appeal for ALS awareness, and he planned to speak to his grandchildren, who had never heard his real voice. The article reports that Francoeur died seven months after the reporter's interview, and it remembers him as a husband and father.

Articles.Title: How AI technology is giving ALS patients their voice back

stories.Headline: Etsy to restrict AI-generated content in effort to combat seller slop
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, October 23, 2026, Etsy announced new restrictions on AI-generated content on its marketplace, citing threats to the integrity of sellers' work and the risk of fraud to buyers. Under the new rules, patterns, recipes, and any other item requiring a buyer to put in effort to finish a product cannot be created with AI. Sellers must also include at least one unaltered photo of the actual item against a real background, and bot-generated listings are banned. AI-generated art remains permitted as long as sellers play a clear role in creating it and are open about their process.

Etsy Vice President of Customer Operations James Ossman wrote in a blog post that the marketplace only works when buyers and sellers trust each other. He said sellers need clear guidance so their creativity and craftsmanship are represented fairly, and buyers need to know what they are purchasing and how much human involvement went into it. Ossman also acknowledged that Etsy has work to do to uphold that standard. The company's note to sellers and Ossman's post both set out these principles, and the article does not report any penalties for violations beyond the removal of illicit listings.

Ossman said Etsy will add a reporting function, similar to one LinkedIn offers, that lets users flag listings with misleading AI imagery. He also said the company will use technology to identify misleading imagery and fraudulent listings, with the goal of expanding removals of illicit listings in the coming months. He added that the company does not yet have every answer on the questions AI raises for its marketplace. Etsy hosts more than 5 million entrepreneurs, most of them women running one-person businesses from home, according to the company's annual report.

The move comes amid an explosion of AI-generated sales content and a growing consumer backlash against what many see as AI slop. Some buyers welcomed the change, including creator Kara Lynne, who said on X that buying a crochet pattern that turned out to be fully AI-generated had been infuriating. Other platforms have responded similarly, with Facebook and Instagram labeling AI content, LinkedIn adding reporting buttons, Snap excluding wholly AI-generated content from its recommendations, and Spotify removing 50 million AI-generated tracks. The article notes that Etsy, with $10.9 billion in goods sales in 2024, is far smaller than Amazon or eBay.

Articles.Title: Etsy to restrict AI-generated content in effort to combat seller slop

stories.Headline: What to Listen For When AI Joins the BSO
stories.Summary:
The Boston Symphony Orchestra will give the world premiere of Tod Machover's "already and not yet" at Symphony Hall from October 22 to 24, with a live artificial intelligence system from the MIT Media Lab performing alongside the orchestra. Conductor Kent Nagano leads the first of three performances on Thursday, and the piece is part of the Boston Musical Intelligencer's coverage of the event. The AI was built by Manaswi Mishra, a PhD researcher at the Media Lab where Machover is faculty director. Mishra trained small models on Machover's recordings of a Vermont river and on river-like sounds developed with the Sejong Soloists, then fed the musicians' live sound into those models during performance.

The AI does not write notes or change the instruments' own sound, since Machover wrote the score and the players produce what is heard from the stage. Instead, the system listens and adds sound through electronics, sometimes stretching a player's line and sometimes answering when Nagano halts the orchestra. The three movements are titled "Smash Up," "Wake Up," and "Stand Up." In the first, loud instruments overwhelm quiet ones, in the second each player gets a short solo that the AI echoes and varies, and in the third the AI draws the players into a shared sound while they decide when to join or diverge. Machover has said the work concerns democracy in peril and the hope for something better, with the orchestra standing in for a society, and he told the Waltham Times he first considered an entirely acoustic piece.

The article's author, a longtime observer of the Boston scene, describes the AI's role in Machover's earlier FLOW Symphony as hard to detect and admires the new work's aims, while noting that the composer and his engineers decide what the machine listens for and whose sound it carries. Machover reportedly says the symphony ends on a question mark because he did not feel it was honest to claim the goal had been reached, which explains the title's "not yet." Nagano opens the program with Mendelssohn's The Hebrides Overture, followed by the US premiere of Alex Nante's Ein feste Burg, and closes with Mendelssohn's Reformation Symphony. On Saturday, Machover talks with George Lewis for that evening's ticket holders, and on Sunday Holly Herndon speaks at MIT, while WCRB broadcasts Saturday's performance.

Articles.Title: What to Listen For When AI Joins the BSO

stories.Headline: 'A cyclical downturn is inevitable' in an AI crash: Strategist Dario Perkins
stories.Summary:
On October 23, 2026, TS Lombard strategist Dario Perkins published a paper titled "Wargaming the AI Crash," modeling what could follow a sharp reversal in technology stocks. He argued that the trigger for such a crash is hard to pinpoint, but that its fallout can be estimated. Perkins projected that US stocks would fall at least 30 percent, wiping out about $20 trillion in market capitalization. He also estimated $125 billion to $200 billion in losses across debt markets and private credit, with a wave of tech-related defaults expected.

Perkins said the weakest parts of the AI ecosystem, including the neoclouds, Oracle, standalone model developers and construction and equipment suppliers, would face acute distress. He said the hyperscalers would suffer serious revenue downgrades, and that a promised cut in capital spending would offer little comfort. He added that traditional banks would not be immune. For the broader economy, he judged that a cyclical downturn is inevitable, with capital spending plunging, confidence evaporating and sizable job losses in construction.

The backdrop to the paper is a difficult October for tech stocks. Concerns began earlier in the month with CoreWeave, whose corporate bonds were sold off amid fears of an AI slowdown, and its shares fell about 35 percent in the month. Meta then posted negative free cash flow in its third-quarter results for the first time since 2012 and said it would issue new stock to fund its AI build-out. Tesla cut its annual capital expenditure plan by $5 billion to $20 billion. On Thursday the Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 2.6 percent, its worst single-day drop since June, and selling persisted into Friday.

Perkins also argued that the downturn would be milder than many expect, at the gentler end of historical recessions, because the AI boom's macroeconomic footprint is smaller than people think and the Federal Reserve has room to cut rates. Miller Tabak strategist Matt Maley said investors who have repeatedly bought the dip in chip stocks may be growing wary. He wondered whether they would stay as aggressive as they have been this year. The articles do not say how markets will respond in the coming weeks.

Articles.Title: 'A cyclical downturn is inevitable' in an AI crash: Strategist Dario Perkins

stories.Headline: Healthcare AI Insights from the SHI Summit
stories.Summary:
Healthcare IT Today published a column by John Lynn on October 23, 2026, summarizing AI insights he gathered at the SHI Summit, hosted by SHI International. Lynn wrote that he attended as a guest of the company and is sharing takeaways that he found useful for the healthcare community. He said he had earlier published a roundup of the cybersecurity content from the same event. The column is a personal commentary rather than a news report of a single event or decision.

Lynn highlighted several points from the conference that bear on healthcare organizations. He noted a statistic repeated at the event that many AI projects are not producing the business outcomes companies want, and he argued that healthcare is somewhat better placed because it tends to be more risk averse and focused on defined outcomes. He also pointed to the speed of AI change as both a concern and an opportunity, and to the risk that training data may miss nuance. He wrote that no single AI platform will solve everything, and that cost matters less than the value an AI investment produces. He added that unsanctioned "shadow AI" use should be treated as a signal of demand, and that a strong chief information security officer is needed so security risks are not overlooked.

Lynn credited SHI International and its CEO, Thai Lee, for their work and for embracing AI, and he thanked the company for hosting him. He presented the points as his own reflections, adding healthcare-specific commentary to content presented by speakers such as Isaac Blake, whose one-liners he quoted. He wrote that healthcare organizations should keep cost discipline and a clear value equation in mind as they adopt AI, even though generating new revenue is harder in healthcare than in other industries. The article closes by inviting readers to share their own views on social media, and it includes no further timeline or planned actions.

Articles.Title: Healthcare AI Insights from the SHI Summit

stories.Headline: The AI sell-off is crushing stocks of companies leading the data center build-out
stories.Summary:
Shares of companies that build and supply AI data centers have been falling sharply even after strong quarterly results, according to a Yahoo Finance report by Jared Blikre published on October 23, 2026. Bloom Energy, which makes fuel cells that generate power on site at data centers, reported that its sales rose 138% last quarter and raised its full-year growth outlook to about 122%. Comfort Systems, which installs cooling and electrical systems, said its backlog nearly doubled to $17.8 billion. Both stocks fell for a second straight day, and Credo, which makes networking parts for data centers, slid with them.

The selling extends well beyond those three names. Since the S&P 500's record close on October 6, the companies building and equipping AI data centers are down a median 23%, based on Yahoo Finance calculations. The group includes Caterpillar, GE Vernova, Vertiv and Eaton, while power producers are down 14% and Nvidia is off 11%. The Big Tech companies writing the checks are down only 5%. Together, a dozen of the largest builders and power companies have lost more than $300 billion in market value since October 6.

Analysts quoted in the report said the main constraint on the build-out is power, and that public pushback against new data centers is adding to the problem. Jefferies analyst Aniket Shah said as much to Yahoo Finance on Wednesday, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly said builders must be good neighbors. Apollo chief economist Torsten Sløk wrote this week that demand for computing power is significantly greater than supply, and he argued that a slower build-out could benefit owners of scarce capacity, such as power producers and transformer makers, where lead times run up to 26 months. The report notes that Yahoo is a portfolio company of funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management.

Sløk also warned that the scarcity could unwind if supply catches up or demand softens, and the report says the market appears to be pricing in that worst case. The article notes that the order books have not yet shown any decline. The next tests come with earnings from Microsoft, Alphabet and Vertiv on Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday, and their spending plans will indicate whether the backlogs keep growing. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The AI sell-off is crushing stocks of companies leading the data center build-out

stories.Headline: Broadcasters Converge on Seychelles to Address AI Challenges
stories.Summary:
The 10th Southern Africa Broadcasters Convention (SABA) opened on Thursday, October 22, at the Avani Barbarons Seychelles Resort, bringing together African broadcasting executives, media practitioners and technology partners. The four-day gathering is co-convened by the Seychelles Broadcasting Corporation (SBC), the Southern Africa Broadcasting Association (SABA) and Broadcast Media Africa, and it is themed "Reimagining Next: AI, Cloud and the Future of Broadcast Media in Africa." The meeting is set to examine how artificial intelligence and cloud technology can improve broadcasting while preserving public trust and human judgement. The article was written by Shuaibu Sambo in Abuja and credited to Voice of Nigeria.

Seychelles Vice-President Sebastien Pillay, who also oversees Information and Communications Technology, declared the convention open. He said broadcasters across the region share problems involving audiences, technology and trust, warning that the same tools that produce accurate reporting can also produce false material quickly and cheaply, making it hard for audiences to tell what is real. He urged African broadcasters to cooperate more closely in sharing skills, tools and content, arguing that smaller countries such as Seychelles could learn from larger organisations. SBC Chief Executive Bérard Duprès said shifting audience habits, including demand for immediacy and engagement across several platforms, are pushing broadcasters to rethink how they deliver content. He said relationships formed at such forums helped SBC launch its radio app, SBC Plus and Digital Terrestrial Television (DTT).

Duprès asked how broadcasters can ensure that technologies such as AI strengthen rather than weaken their public service mandates. He noted that AI can assist with content production but that broadcasters must keep control of the stories they tell and the authenticity that connects them with audiences. Speaking for SABA, Eswatini TV Chief Executive Mlamuli Dlamini said technological change must stay guided by human creativity and editorial responsibility. Representatives of the Voice of Nigeria and the Tanzanian Broadcasting Corporation are among the executives from other parts of Africa attending the convention.

Articles.Title: Broadcasters Converge on Seychelles to Address AI Challenges

stories.Headline: AI could transform risk management for producers
stories.Summary:
The chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Michael Selig, has said that artificial intelligence is expected to play a larger role in agriculture, including in helping farmers and ranchers make risk management decisions. The remarks were reported by Brownfield Ag News reporter Kellan Heavican on October 23, 2026. Selig said AI is already being used in production agriculture and will likely have a role in trading and pricing commodity futures. The article does not describe any new rule, requirement or formal change. Selig told Brownfield that AI-generated tools could help producers decide when to take out a risk management position, how to manage that risk, and how to receive trading advice without relying on an intermediary.

He argued that automating parts of this process could improve efficiency and timing for producers. He also suggested that the current regulatory approach to brokers makes market access costly for farmers, ranchers and producers who use the markets each day. Selig said that automation could produce cost savings. Selig said that whenever new technology is adopted into a sector, it can disrupt the marketplace at first, but that over time the change improves the market. The article attributes these views to Selig himself and does not include comments from other regulators, industry groups or producers.

It does not give figures on expected savings or a timeline for adoption. The article also offers no details on how any of these ideas would be put into practice. The piece sits alongside other Brownfield coverage of farm market conditions, including reports on cash dairy prices and livestock markets from the same week. The article does not say whether the CFTC plans any specific action on AI in agricultural trading, and it does not describe next steps beyond the chairman's comments.

Articles.Title: AI could transform risk management for producers

stories.Headline: I Pitted a Human Coach Against an AI Platform for my Last Half. Guess Which One Gave Me Crazy Advice?
stories.Summary:
This is a feature piece rather than breaking news, so the three-to-four paragraph structure applies. The article has enough material to cover the comparison, but I must be careful: the source describes the author's personal experiment and includes many specifics. Writing this version with exactly four or five sentences per paragraph. Claire Trageser, a long-time runner, tested two very different ways of training for a half marathon, first with a human coach and then with an AI coaching app. Her human coach, Brian Maiorano, charges $120 a month and builds two-week training blocks using a tracking platform, then reviews her performance by email.

The AI app, Runna, costs about $10 a month and generates a four-month plan that adjusts based on completed workouts and runner feedback. The story was published on October 23, 2026, by Outside's RUN section, and it reflects one runner's personal experience rather than a controlled study. Trageser stresses that the two races were not comparable in conditions, so her conclusions focus on the experience rather than the results. The most striking difference came early with the AI plan, which included a "rolling 800s" workout at 6:35 per mile, a pace she said was faster than her 5K time.

She gave up partway through and jogged home, later texting a friend that the app was "trying to kill" her. After that session, Runna quickly suggested less aggressive paces and rebuilt the plan. Trageser felt her pride was hurt and questioned whether one hard workout fairly predicted her half marathon pace. Runna's head coach, Steph Kessell, told her the plans are meant to adapt, using data from completed sessions and user feedback such as "Not Feeling 100%."

Maiorano, by contrast, eased Trageser into intervals and adjusted her plan based on her responses, lowering paces or reducing mileage when she struggled. He said software serves only as a rough guideline for him, and that his experience overrides it when an athlete's splits or remarks suggest otherwise. He argued that coaching involves trust, goal setting, injury prevention and encouragement, and that a human coach cares about the outcome in a way an app cannot. Trageser said her desire not to disappoint him drove her to push harder, and she finished her human-coached race with a small personal record.

The article also notes that Maiorano himself uses AI only as a chatting partner for exploring training ideas, not for writing workouts. The piece frames the comparison as one of accountability more than raw performance, and it leaves the broader debate about AI coaching open. Trageser concludes that an app may suit runners who need only a schedule, while people who want emotional investment and personal trust may still value a human coach. The article does not offer a definitive verdict on which approach produces better results over the long term.

Articles.Title: I Pitted a Human Coach Against an AI Platform for my Last Half. Guess Which One Gave Me Crazy Advice?

stories.Headline: AI gets people into trouble in the backcountry
stories.Summary:
Three hikers who relied partly on Google's Gemini chatbot got into trouble on Mount Shasta in Northern California, where they called for help from a rocky face after summiting at 7:30 p.m. and having to descend in the dark. They had brought too little food, overestimated their fitness, and by morning were lost on a difficult section of the mountain, with one hiker injuring his knee. The Forest Service's Nick Meyers, who runs the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center that responded, said the group had at least tried to prepare but seemed to have stopped thinking for themselves.

Similar cases were reported elsewhere, including a visitor who camped beside a "No Camping" sign because an AI told her she could, and a man at a trailhead carrying an AI-generated map with features on the wrong side of a mountain. In British Columbia, a helicopter crew rescued a 16-year-old from a ledge on Crown Mountain after he used Anthropic's Claude to help plan the trip, though he also consulted Google Maps and AllTrails. Grand Teton National Park has seen a sharp rise in visitors who say they use AI for travel information, with Superintendent Chip Jenkins reporting a jump from zero to 26 percent over the past year. Meyers said it remains unclear whether this will raise accidents and rescues, noting his office averages about a dozen rescues a year and 2026 looks average so far.

Wyoming's search and rescue calls have actually fallen, with 312 calls so far in 2026 compared with 466 in 2025 and 377 in 2024. Some rescue veterans point out that social media and Google Maps caused similar problems in earlier years. Experts add that chatbots can state errors with confidence and tell users what they want to hear. Chris Flathmann, a human-centered computing professor at Clemson University who has studied AI and search and rescue, warned of "cognitive surrender," in which people stop thinking critically once they lean heavily on an AI system.

He said a chatbot posing as an expert is hard to challenge when the user lacks expertise, and that such habits are difficult to break in stressful conditions. Jim Moss, a Colorado recreation attorney and search and rescue volunteer, noted that greater outdoor recreation overall has also increased the number of people at risk. The experts advise checking any AI-provided information against up-to-date public-land agency maps, trail association sites, guidebooks, or a park ranger. Meyers summed up the point by saying that anyone heading into dangerous places should take planning seriously.

Articles.Title: AI gets people into trouble in the backcountry

stories.Headline: Bridging the AI Execution Gap: Salesforce and AWS Reengineer Enterprise Tech Delivery for Indian CXOs - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a podcast episode from ETCIO, published on 23 October 2026, in which host Vaishnavi J Desai talked with Mankiran Chowhan, Managing Director at Salesforce India, and Sandeep Dutta, President for India and South Asia at AWS.
